"That's just it, exactly," Princess Myakaya turned to him. "But the point is that I won't abandon Anna to your mercies. She's so nice, so charming. How can she help it if they're all in love with her and follow her about like shadows?"
"Oh, I had no idea of blaming her for it," Anna's friend said in self-defense.
"If no one follows us about like a shadow, that's no proof we have any right to blame her."

And, having duly disposed of Anna's friend, Princess Myakaya got up and, together with the ambassador's wife, joined the group at the table, where the conversation was dealing with the king of Prussia.
"What wicked gossip were you talking over there?" Betsy asked.
"About the Karenins. The princess gave us a sketch of Alexey Alexandrovitch," said the ambassador's wife with a smile, as she sat down at the table.
"A pity we didn't hear it!" Princess Betsy said, glancing toward the door. "Ah, here you are at last!" she said, turning with a smile to Vronsky as he came in.

Vronsky was not merely acquainted with everyone he was meeting here; he saw them all every day, and so he came in with the quiet manner with which one enters a room full of people from whom one has only just parted.

"Where do I come from?" he said, in answer to a question from the ambassador's wife. "Well, there's no help for it, I must confess. From the _opera bouffe_. I do believe I've seen it a hundred times, and always with fresh enjoyment. It's exquisite. I know it's disgraceful, but I fall asleep at the opera, and I sit through the _opera bouffe_ to the last minute and enjoy it. This evening..."
He mentioned a French actress and was about to tell something about her; but the ambassador's wife, with playful horror, cut him short.
"Please don't tell us about that horror."
"All right, I won't — especially as everyone knows those horrors."
"And we'd all go see them if it were accepted as the correct thing, like the opera," Princess Myakaya chimed in.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Steps were heard at the door, and Princess Betsy, knowing it was Madame Karenina, glanced at Vronsky. He was looking toward the door, and his face wore a strange new expression. Joyfully, intently, and at the same time timidly, he gazed at the approaching figure, and slowly rose to his feet. Anna walked into the drawing-room. Holding herself extremely erect, as always, looking straight ahead, and moving with that swift, decisive, and light step that set her apart from all other society women, she crossed the short space to her hostess, shook hands with her, smiled, and with the same smile looked round at Vronsky. Vronsky bowed low and pushed up a chair for her.
She acknowledged this only with a slight nod, flushed a little, and frowned. But at once, while rapidly greeting her acquaintances and shaking the hands held out to her, she turned to Princess Betsy:
"I've been at Countess Lidia's, and meant to come here earlier, but I stayed on. Sir John was there. He's very interesting."
"Oh, that's this missionary?"
"Yes — he told us about life in India, the most interesting things."
The conversation, which her arrival had interrupted, flickered up again like the flame of a lamp being blown out.
"Sir John! Yes, Sir John; I've met him. He's a good speaker. The Vlassieva girl is quite in love with him."
"And is it true the younger Vlassieva girl's to marry Topov?"
"Yes, they say it's all but settled."
"I'm amazed at the parents! They say it's a marriage for love."
"For love? What antediluvian notions you have! Who talks of love in these days?" said the ambassador's wife.
"What can one do? It's a foolish old fashion that's still kept up," Vronsky said.
"So much the worse for those who keep up the fashion. The only happy marriages I know are marriages of prudence."
"Yes, but how often the happiness of these prudent marriages flies away like dust, simply because the very passion they refused to recognize turns up," Vronsky said.
"But by marriages of prudence we mean those in which both parties have already sown their wild oats. It's like scarlatina — you have to go through it and get it over with."
"Then they ought to find out how to vaccinate for love, like smallpox."
"In my young days I was in love with a deacon," said Princess Myakaya. "I don't know that it did me any good."
"No — I imagine, joking aside, that to know love, one has to make mistakes and then correct them," said Princess Betsy.
"Even after marriage?" the ambassador's wife asked playfully.
"'It's never too late to mend.'" The attaché repeated the English proverb.

"Just so," Betsy agreed; "one has to make mistakes and correct them. What do you think about it?" she turned to Anna, who, with a faintly visible resolute smile on her lips, was listening to the conversation in silence.
"I think," Anna said, toying with the glove she had taken off, "I think... so many men, so many minds; certainly so many hearts, so many kinds of love."
Vronsky was gazing at Anna, waiting with a sinking heart for what she would say. He sighed as though after a danger had been escaped when she uttered these words.
Anna suddenly turned to him.
"Oh, I had a letter from Moscow. They write me that Kitty Shtcherbatskaya is very ill."
"Really?" Vronsky said, frowning.
Anna looked sternly at him.
"Doesn't that interest you?"
"On the contrary, very much. What was it exactly they told you, if I may know?" he asked.
Anna got up and went over to Betsy.
"Give me a cup of tea," she said, standing at her table.
While Betsy was pouring the tea, Vronsky went up to Anna.
"What is it they're writing to you?" he repeated.

"I often think men have no understanding of what isn't honorable, though they're always talking about it," Anna said, without answering him. "I've been wanting to tell you this for a long while," she added, and moving a few steps away, sat down at a table in a corner covered with albums.
"I don't quite understand what you mean," he said, handing her the cup.
She glanced toward the sofa beside her, and he instantly sat down.
"Yes, I've been meaning to tell you," she said, not looking at him. "You behaved wrongly — very wrongly."
"Do you suppose I don't know I've acted wrongly? But who was the cause of my doing so?"
"Why are you saying that to me?" she asked, glancing severely at him.
"You know why," he answered boldly and joyfully, meeting her gaze and not lowering his eyes.
It was not he, but she, who was flustered.
"That just shows you have no heart," she said. But her eyes said that she knew he did have a heart, and that was the very reason she was afraid of him.
"What you spoke of just now was a mistake, and not love."

"Remember that I have forbidden you to utter that word, that hateful word," Anna said with a shudder. But at once she felt that by the very word "forbidden" she had betrayed that she acknowledged certain rights over him, and was, by that very fact, encouraging him to speak of love. "I've long meant to tell you this," she went on, looking firmly into his eyes, hot all over from the burning flush on her cheeks. "I came on purpose this evening, knowing I'd meet you. I have come to tell you that this must end. I have never blushed in front of anyone, and you force me to feel guilty of something."
He looked at her and was struck by a new spiritual beauty in her face.
"What do you want of me?" he asked simply and gravely.
"I want you to go to Moscow and ask Kitty's forgiveness," she said.
"You don't really want that?" he said.
He saw that she was saying what she forced herself to say, not what she wanted to say.
"If you love me, as you say," she whispered, "then act so that I may have peace."
His face lit up.

"Don't you know you are my whole life? But I know no peace, and I can't give it to you; all of myself — and love... yes. I can't think of you and myself apart. You and I are one to me. And I see no chance of peace ahead — either for me or for you. I see a chance of despair, of wretchedness... or a chance of bliss — what bliss!... Can it really be that there's no chance of it?" he murmured with his lips; but she heard.
She strained every effort of her mind to say what ought to be said. But instead she let her eyes rest on him, full of love, and made no answer.
"It's come!" he thought in ecstasy. "When I was beginning to despair, when it seemed there would be no end — it's come! She loves me. She admits it!"
"Then do this for me: never say such things to me again, and let's be friends," she said in words; but her eyes spoke quite differently.
"Friends we shall never be — you know that yourself. Whether we shall be the happiest or the most wretched of people — that's in your hands."
She would have said something, but he interrupted.

"I ask one thing only: I ask for the right to hope, to suffer as I do. But if even that cannot be, then order me to disappear, and I disappear. If my presence is hateful to you, you shall not see me."
"I don't want to drive you away."
"Only don't change anything — leave everything as it is," he said in a shaky voice. "Here's your husband."
At that very instant Alexey Alexandrovitch did in fact walk into the room with his calm, awkward gait.

Glancing at his wife and Vronsky, he went over to the lady of the house and, sitting down for a cup of tea, started talking in his deliberate, always audible voice, in his usual mocking tone, ridiculing someone.
"Your Rambouillet is in full conclave," he said, looking round at all the party — "the graces and the muses."

But Princess Betsy could not endure that tone of his — "sneering," as she called it, using the English word — and like a skillful hostess she at once drew him into a serious conversation on the subject of universal conscription. Alexey Alexandrovitch was immediately interested in the subject and began earnestly defending the new imperial decree against Princess Betsy, who had attacked it.
Vronsky and Anna still sat at the little table.
"This is getting indecorous," whispered one lady, with an expressive glance at Madame Karenina, Vronsky, and her husband.
"What did I tell you?" said Anna's friend.

But it was not only those ladies; almost everyone in the room, even Princess Myakaya and Betsy herself, glanced several times in the direction of the two who had withdrawn from the general circle, as though it were a disturbing fact. Alexey Alexandrovitch was the only one who did not once look in that direction, and was not diverted from the interesting discussion he had entered into.
Noticing the unpleasant impression being made on everyone, Princess Betsy slipped someone else into her seat to listen to Alexey Alexandrovitch, and went over to Anna.
"I'm always amazed at the clarity and precision of your husband's language," she said. "The most transcendent ideas seem to be within my grasp when he's speaking."
"Oh, yes!" said Anna, radiant with a smile of happiness, and not understanding a word of what Betsy had said. She crossed over to the big table and joined in the general conversation.

Alexey Alexandrovitch, after staying half an hour, went up to his wife and suggested they go home together. But she answered, not looking at him, that she was staying for supper. Alexey Alexandrovitch made his bows and withdrew.

The fat old Tatar, Madame Karenina's coachman, was having trouble holding one of her pair of grays, which was chilled and rearing at the entrance. A footman stood holding the carriage door open. The hall-porter held open the great door of the house. Anna Arkadyevna, with her quick little hand, was unfastening the lace of her sleeve, which had caught in the hook of her fur cloak, and with her head bent was listening to the words Vronsky was murmuring as he escorted her down.

"You've said nothing, of course, and I ask nothing," he was saying; "but you know that friendship is not what I want — that there's only one happiness in life for me, that word you dislike so... yes, love!"

"Love," she repeated slowly, in an inner voice, and suddenly, at the very instant she unhooked the lace, she added, "Why I don't like the word is that it means too much to me, far more than you can understand," and she glanced into his face. "_Au revoir!_"
She gave him her hand, and with her rapid, springy step she passed by the porter and vanished into the carriage.

The glance, the brush of her hand, set him on fire. He kissed the palm where she had touched him, and went home, happy with the sense that this evening had brought him closer to his goal than the last two months put together.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had seen nothing striking or improper in the fact that his wife had been sitting with Vronsky at a separate table, in eager conversation with him about something. But he noticed that to the rest of the party it appeared striking and improper, and for that reason it seemed improper to him as well. He made up his mind that he must speak to his wife about it.

On reaching home, Alexey Alexandrovitch went to his study, as he usually did, sat down in his low chair, opened a book on the Papacy to the place where he had laid the paper-knife in it, and read until one o'clock, just as he usually did. But from time to time he rubbed his high forehead and shook his head, as though to drive away something. At his usual time he got up and got ready for bed. Anna Arkadyevna had not yet come in. With a book under his arm he went upstairs. But this evening, instead of his usual thoughts and meditations on official details, his thoughts were absorbed by his wife and something unpleasant connected with her. Contrary to his usual habit, he did not get into bed but fell to walking up and down the rooms with his hands clasped behind his back. He could not go to bed, feeling it was absolutely necessary for him first to think thoroughly through the situation that had just arisen.

When Alexey Alexandrovitch had decided he had to talk to his wife about it, it had seemed a very easy and simple thing. But now, as he began to think over the question that had just arisen, it appeared very complicated and difficult.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was not a jealous man. Jealousy according to his notions was an insult to one's wife, and one ought to have confidence in one's wife. Why one ought to have confidence — that is, complete conviction that his young wife would always love him — he did not ask himself. But he had no experience of a lack of confidence, because he had confidence in her, and told himself that he ought to. Now, although his conviction that jealousy was a shameful feeling and that one ought to feel confidence had not broken down, he felt that he was standing face to face with something illogical and irrational, and did not know what to do. Alexey Alexandrovitch was standing face to face with life — with the possibility of his wife loving someone other than himself — and this seemed to him very irrational and incomprehensible, because it was life itself. All his life Alexey Alexandrovitch had lived and worked in official spheres, having to do with the reflection of life. And every time he had stumbled against life itself he had shrunk from it. Now he felt something akin to what a man might feel who, while calmly crossing a chasm by a bridge, suddenly discovers that the bridge is broken, and that there is a chasm below. That chasm was life itself; the bridge was the artificial life in which Alexey Alexandrovitch had been living. For the first time the question of the possibility of his wife's loving someone else presented itself to him, and he was horrified at it.

He did not undress, but walked up and down with his regular tread over the resounding parquet of the dining-room — where one lamp was burning — over the carpet of the dark drawing-room, where the light was reflected on the big new portrait of himself hanging over the sofa, and across her boudoir, where two candles were burning, lighting up the portraits of her parents and women friends and the pretty knick-knacks on her writing-table that he knew so well. He walked across her boudoir to the bedroom door and turned back again. At each turn in his walk, especially on the parquet of the lit dining-room, he halted and said to himself, "Yes, I must decide this and put a stop to it; I must express my view of it and my decision." And he turned back again. "But express what — what decision?" he asked himself in the drawing-room, and could find no reply. "But after all," he asked himself before turning into the boudoir, "what has happened? Nothing. She talked a long while with him. But what of that? Surely women in society can talk to whom they please. And then, jealousy lowers both me and her," he told himself as he went into her boudoir; but this dictum, which had always carried such weight with him before, now had no weight and no meaning at all. And from the bedroom door he turned back again; but as he entered the dark drawing-room some inner voice told him that this was not so, and that if others had noticed it, that showed there was something. And he said to himself again in the dining-room, "Yes, I must decide and put a stop to it, and express my view of it..." And again at the turn in the drawing-room he asked himself, "Decide how?" And again he asked himself, "What has happened?" and answered, "Nothing," and reminded himself that jealousy was a feeling insulting to his wife; but again in the drawing-room he was convinced that something had happened. His thoughts, like his body, went round a complete circle without coming upon anything new. He noticed this, rubbed his forehead, and sat down in her boudoir.

There, looking at her table with the malachite blotting case lying on top and an unfinished letter, his thoughts suddenly shifted. He began to think of her, of what she was thinking and feeling. For the first time he pictured to himself vividly her personal life, her ideas, her wishes, and the idea that she could and should have a separate life of her own struck him as so alarming that he hurried to dispel it. It was the chasm he was afraid to peer into. To put himself, in thought and feeling, in another person's place was a spiritual exercise not natural to Alexey Alexandrovitch. He regarded this spiritual exercise as a harmful and dangerous abuse of the imagination.

"And the worst of it all," he thought, "is that just now, at the very moment when my great work is approaching completion" (he was thinking of the project he was putting forward at that time), "when I need all my mental peace and all my energy, just now this stupid worry has to fall on me. But what's to be done? I'm not one of those men who submit to uneasiness and worry without having the strength of character to face them."
"I must think it over, come to a decision, and put it out of my mind," he said aloud.

"The question of her feelings, of what has happened and may be happening in her soul, is not my affair; that's the affair of her conscience and falls under the head of religion," he said to himself, taking consolation in the sense that he had found the division of regulating principles under which this new circumstance properly belonged.

"And so," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself, "questions about her feelings and so on are questions for her conscience, with which I can have nothing to do. My duty is clearly defined. As the head of the family, I am the person bound in duty to guide her, and so, in part, the person responsible; I am bound to point out the danger I see, to warn her — even to use my authority. I must speak plainly to her." And everything he would say tonight to his wife took clear shape in Alexey Alexandrovitch's head. Thinking over what he would say, he somewhat regretted that he should have to use his time and mental powers for domestic consumption, with so little to show for it; but in spite of that, the form and content of the speech before him shaped itself as clearly and distinctly in his head as a ministerial report.

"I must lay out fully the following points: first, the value to be attached to public opinion and to decorum; secondly, the religious significance of marriage; thirdly, if need be, the calamity that may follow for our son; fourthly, the unhappiness likely to result for herself." And, interlacing his fingers, Alexey Alexandrovitch stretched them, and the joints cracked. This trick, a bad habit — the cracking of his fingers — always soothed him, and gave precision to his thoughts, which he so badly needed now.
There was the sound of a carriage driving up to the front door. Alexey Alexandrovitch halted in the middle of the room.

A woman's step was heard climbing the stairs. Alexey Alexandrovitch, his speech at the ready, stood with his crossed fingers pressed together, waiting to see whether another crack would come. One joint cracked.
Already from the sound of light steps on the stairs he could tell she was close, and though pleased with his speech, he felt frightened of the explanation that lay ahead of him...

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Anna came in with hanging head, playing with the tassels of her hood. Her face was brilliant and glowing; but this glow was not one of brightness — it suggested the fearful glow of a fire burning in the middle of a dark night. When she saw her husband, Anna raised her head and smiled, as though she had just woken up.

"You're not in bed? What a wonder!" she said, letting fall her hood, and without stopping she went on into the dressing-room. "It's late, Alexey Alexandrovitch," she said, when she had gone through the doorway.
"Anna, I need to have a talk with you."

"With me?" she said in surprise. She came out from behind the door of the dressing-room and looked at him. "Why — what is it? What about?" she asked, sitting down. "Well, let's talk, if it's so necessary. But it would be better to go to sleep."

Anna said whatever came to her lips, and was astonished, hearing herself, at her own capacity for lying. How simple and natural her words were, and how plausible that she was simply sleepy! She felt clad in an impenetrable armor of falsehood. She felt that some unseen force had come to her aid and was sustaining her.
"Anna, I must warn you," he began.
"Warn me?" she said. "Of what?"

She looked at him so simply, so brightly, that anyone who did not know her as her husband knew her could not have noticed anything unnatural — either in the sound or the sense of her words. But to him, knowing her, knowing that whenever he went to bed five minutes later than usual she noticed it and asked him why; knowing that every joy, every pleasure, every pain she felt she communicated to him at once — to him, to see now that she did not care to notice his state of mind, that she did not care to say a word about herself, meant a great deal. He saw that the innermost recesses of her soul, which until now had always lain open before him, were closed against him. More than that, he saw from her tone that she was not even perturbed at that, but as it were said straight out to him: "Yes, it's shut up, and so it must be, and will be from now on." Now he felt something a man might feel returning home and finding his own house locked up. "But perhaps the key may still be found," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought.

"I want to warn you," he said in a low voice, "that through thoughtlessness and lack of caution you may give people cause to talk about you in society. Your too animated conversation this evening with Count Vronsky" (he pronounced the name firmly and with deliberate emphasis) "attracted attention."
He talked and looked at her laughing eyes, which now frightened him with their impenetrable look, and as he spoke he felt all the uselessness and emptiness of his words.

"You're always like that," she answered, as though she had completely misunderstood him and had taken in only his last phrase. "One time you don't like my being dull, another time you don't like my being lively. I wasn't dull. Does that offend you?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch shivered, and bent his hands to make the joints crack.
"Oh, please, don't do that, I do so dislike it," she said.
"Anna, is this really you?" Alexey Alexandrovitch said, quietly mastering himself and restraining the motion of his fingers.
"But what is all this about?" she said, with such genuine and droll surprise. "What do you want of me?"

Alexey Alexandrovitch paused, and rubbed his forehead and his eyes. He saw that, instead of doing what he had intended — that is, warning his wife against a mistake in the eyes of the world — he had unconsciously become agitated over what was the business of her conscience, and was struggling against the barrier he fancied between them.

"Here's what I meant to say to you," he went on coldly and composedly, "and I beg you to listen. As you know, I consider jealousy a humiliating and degrading feeling, and I shall never let myself be governed by it; but there are certain rules of decorum that cannot be disregarded without consequence. This evening it was not I who noticed it, but, judging by the impression on the company, everyone noticed that your conduct and bearing were not altogether what one would wish."

"I positively don't understand," Anna said, shrugging. "He doesn't care," she thought. "But other people noticed, and that's what upsets him." — "You're not well, Alexey Alexandrovitch," she added, and got up, and would have gone toward the door; but he moved forward as though he would stop her.
His face was ugly and forbidding in a way Anna had never seen before. She stopped, and bending her head back and to one side, set to work taking out her hairpins with her quick hand.
"Well, I'm listening for what's to come," she said calmly and ironically; "and indeed I'll listen with interest, for I should like to understand what the matter is."
She spoke, and marveled at the confident, calm, natural tone in which she was speaking, and at her choice of words.

"To enter into all the details of your feelings I have no right, and besides I consider it useless and even harmful," Alexey Alexandrovitch began. "Ferreting in one's soul, one often ferrets out something that might have lain there unnoticed. Your feelings are an affair of your own conscience; but I am in duty bound to you, to myself, and to God to point out your duties to you. Our lives have been joined, not by man, but by God. That union can only be severed by a crime, and a crime of that nature brings its own punishment."
"I don't understand a word of it. And, oh dear, how sleepy I am — unluckily," she said, rapidly running her hand through her hair, feeling for the remaining hairpins.
"Anna, for God's sake don't speak like that!" he said gently. "Perhaps I'm mistaken, but believe me, what I say I say as much for myself as for you. I am your husband, and I love you."

For an instant her face fell, and the mocking gleam in her eyes died away; but the word _love_ threw her into revolt again. She thought: "Love? Can he love? If he had never heard there was such a thing as love, he would never have used the word. He doesn't even know what love is."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch, really I don't understand," she said. "Define what it is you find..."

"Pardon — let me say all I have to say. I love you. But I'm not speaking of myself; the most important people in this matter are our son and yourself. It may well be, I repeat, that my words will seem to you utterly unnecessary and out of place; it may be that they are called forth by my mistaken impression. In that case, I beg you to forgive me. But if you yourself are conscious of even the smallest grounds for them, then I beg you to think a little, and if your heart prompts you, to speak openly to me..."
Alexey Alexandrovitch was unconsciously saying something utterly unlike what he had prepared.
"I have nothing to say. And besides," she said hurriedly, with difficulty repressing a smile, "it's really time to be in bed."
Alexey Alexandrovitch sighed, and, without saying more, went into the bedroom.

When she came into the bedroom, he was already in bed. His lips were sternly compressed, and his eyes looked away from her. Anna got into her bed and lay waiting, expecting any minute that he would begin to speak to her again. She both feared his speaking and wished for it. But he was silent. She waited a long while without moving, and had forgotten about him. She thought of that other man; she pictured him, and felt how her heart was flooded with emotion and guilty delight at the thought of him. Suddenly she heard an even, tranquil snore. For the first instant Alexey Alexandrovitch seemed, as it were, appalled at his own snoring, and stopped; but after an interval of two breaths the snore sounded again, in a new, tranquil rhythm.
"It's late, it's late," she whispered with a smile. For a long while she lay there motionless, her eyes open; in the darkness she almost imagined she could see their brilliance.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: From that time a new life began for Alexey Alexandrovitch and his wife. Nothing in particular happened. Anna went out into society as she had always done, was especially often at Princess Betsy's, and met Vronsky everywhere. Alexey Alexandrovitch saw this, but could do nothing about it. All his efforts to draw her into open discussion she met with a barrier he could not penetrate, made up of a kind of amused perplexity. Outwardly everything was the same, but their inner relations had completely changed. Alexey Alexandrovitch, a man of great power in the world of politics, felt himself helpless in this. Like an ox with its head bent, he submissively awaited the blow that he sensed was raised over him. Every time he began to think about it, he felt he must try once more, that by kindness, tenderness, and persuasion there was still hope of saving her, of bringing her back to herself, and every day he prepared to talk to her. But every time he began to talk to her, he felt that the spirit of evil and deception that had taken possession of her had possession of him too, and he spoke to her in a tone quite unlike that in which he had meant to speak. In spite of himself he addressed her in his habitual tone of jeering at anyone who would say what he was saying. And in that tone it was impossible to say what needed to be said to her.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: What for Vronsky had been almost a whole year the one absorbing desire of his life, replacing all his old desires; what for Anna had been an impossible, terrible, and for that very reason all the more entrancing dream of bliss — that desire had been fulfilled. He stood before her, pale, his lower jaw quivering, and begged her to be calm, not knowing how or why.
"Anna! Anna!" he said in a choked voice, "Anna, for pity's sake!..."

But the louder he spoke, the lower she dropped her once proud and gay, now shame-stricken head, and she bowed down and sank from the sofa where she was sitting, down onto the floor at his feet; she would have fallen on the carpet if he had not held her.
"My God! Forgive me!" she said, sobbing, pressing his hands to her bosom.

She felt so sinful, so guilty, that nothing was left for her but to humble herself and beg forgiveness; and as now there was no one in her life but him, it was to him that she addressed her prayer for forgiveness. Looking at him, she had a physical sense of her humiliation, and she could say nothing more. He felt what a murderer must feel when he sees the body he has robbed of life. That body — robbed by him of life — was their love, the first stage of their love. There was something awful and revolting in the memory of what had been bought at this fearful price of shame. Shame at their spiritual nakedness crushed her and infected him. But, for all the murderer's horror before the body of his victim, he must hack it to pieces, hide it, must make use of what he has gained by his murder.

And with fury, almost with passion, the murderer falls on the body and drags and hacks at it; so he covered her face and shoulders with kisses. She held his hand and did not move. "Yes, these kisses — this is what has been bought by this shame. Yes, and one hand, which will always be mine — the hand of my accomplice." She lifted that hand and kissed it. He sank to his knees and tried to see her face; but she hid it, and said nothing. At last, as though making an effort over herself, she got up and pushed him away. Her face was still as beautiful, but only the more pitiful for that.
"All is over," she said; "I have nothing but you. Remember that."
"I can never forget what is my whole life. For one instant of this happiness..."
"Happiness!" she said with horror and loathing, and her horror unconsciously infected him. "For pity's sake, not a word, not a word more."
She rose quickly and moved away from him.

"Not a word more," she repeated, and with a look of chill despair, incomprehensible to him, she parted from him. She felt that at that moment she could not put into words the sense of shame, of rapture, and of horror at stepping into a new life, and she did not want to speak of it, to vulgarize this feeling with inappropriate words. But later, too, and the next day and the third day, she still found no words in which to express the complexity of her feelings; indeed, she could not even find thoughts in which to clearly think out all that was in her soul.

She told herself: "No, just now I can't think about it, later on, when I'm calmer." But this calm for thought never came; every time the thought rose up of what she had done and what would happen to her and what she ought to do, a horror came over her and she drove those thoughts away.
"Later, later," she said — "when I'm calmer."

But in dreams, when she had no control over her thoughts, her position presented itself to her in all its hideous nakedness. One dream haunted her almost every night. She dreamed that both men were her husbands at once, that both were lavishing caresses on her. Alexey Alexandrovitch was weeping, kissing her hands, and saying, "How happy we are now!" And Alexey Vronsky was there too, and he too was her husband. And she was marveling that it had once seemed impossible to her, was explaining to them, laughing, that this was ever so much simpler, that now both of them were happy and content. But this dream weighed on her like a nightmare, and she would wake from it in terror.

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: In the early days after his return from Moscow, whenever Levin shuddered and grew red, remembering the disgrace of his rejection, he would say to himself: "This was just how I used to shudder and blush, thinking myself utterly lost, when I was plucked in physics and didn't get my remove; and how I thought myself utterly ruined after I had bungled that affair of my sister's that was entrusted to me. And yet, now that years have passed, I look back on it and wonder that it could have distressed me so much. It will be the same with this trouble. Time will pass and I won't mind about this either."

But three months had passed and he had not stopped minding about it; and it was as painful for him to think of it as it had been those first days. He could not be at peace because, after dreaming for so long of family life and feeling himself so ripe for it, he was still not married, and was further than ever from marriage. He was painfully aware himself, as were all around him, that at his age it is not good for a man to be alone. He remembered how before leaving for Moscow he had once said to his cowman Nikolay, a simple-hearted peasant whom he liked to talk to: "Well, Nikolay! I mean to get married," and how Nikolay had promptly answered, as though it were a matter beyond any doubt: "And high time too, Konstantin Dmitrievitch." But marriage had now become further off than ever. The place was taken, and whenever he tried to imagine any of the girls he knew in that place, he felt it was utterly impossible. Moreover, the memory of the rejection and the part he had played in the affair tortured him with shame. However often he told himself he was in no way to blame for it, that memory, like other humiliating recollections of a similar kind, made him twinge and blush. There had been in his past, as in every man's, actions recognized by him as bad, for which his conscience ought to have tormented him; but the memory of these bad actions caused him nothing like as much suffering as those trivial but humiliating recollections. These wounds never healed. And alongside these memories was now ranged his rejection and the pitiful figure he must have cut to others that evening. But time and work did their part. Bitter memories were increasingly covered over by the incidents — petty in his eyes, but actually important — of his country life. Every week he thought less often of Kitty. He was impatiently waiting for the news that she was married, or just about to be, hoping that such news would, like having a tooth out, completely cure him.

Meanwhile spring came on, beautiful and kindly, without the delays and treacheries of spring — one of those rare springs in which plants, beasts, and man rejoice alike. This lovely spring roused Levin still more, and strengthened him in his resolution to renounce all his past and build up his lonely life firmly and independently. Though many of the plans with which he had returned to the country had not been carried out, his most important resolution — that of purity — had been kept. He was free of the shame that had usually harassed him after a fall; and he could look everyone straight in the face. In February he had received a letter from Marya Nikolaevna saying that his brother Nikolay's health was getting worse, but that he would not take advice, and on the strength of this letter Levin went to Moscow to his brother's and succeeded in persuading him to see a doctor and to go to a watering-place abroad. He succeeded so well in persuading his brother, and in lending him money for the trip without irritating him, that he was pleased with himself on that score. Beyond his farming, which called for special attention in spring, and beyond his reading, Levin had begun that winter a work on agriculture, the plan of which turned on taking into account the character of the laborer on the land as one of the unalterable givens of the question, like the climate and the soil, and consequently deducing all the principles of scientific cultivation not simply from the data of soil and climate, but from the data of soil, climate, and a certain unalterable character of the laborer. Thus, in spite of his solitude, or because of it, his life was exceedingly full. Only rarely did he suffer from an unsatisfied desire to share his stray ideas with someone besides Agafea Mihalovna. With her, indeed, he not infrequently fell into discussions on physics, the theory of agriculture, and especially philosophy; philosophy was Agafea Mihalovna's favorite subject.

Spring was slow in unfolding. For the last few weeks the weather had been steadily fine and frosty. In the daytime it thawed in the sun, but at night there were even seven degrees of frost. There was such a frozen crust on the snow that they could drive the wagons anywhere off the roads. Easter came in the snow. Then all of a sudden, on Easter Monday, a warm wind sprang up, storm clouds swooped down, and for three days and three nights the warm, driving rain fell in streams. On Thursday the wind dropped, and a thick gray fog brooded over the land as though hiding the mysteries of the transformations being wrought in nature. Behind the fog there was the flowing of water, the cracking and floating of ice, the swift rush of turbid, foaming torrents; and on the following Monday, in the evening, the fog parted, the storm clouds split into little curling crests, the sky cleared, and the real spring had come. In the morning the sun rose brilliant and quickly wore away the thin layer of ice covering the water, and all the warm air was quivering with steam rising from the quickening earth. The old grass looked greener, and the young grass thrust up its tiny blades; the buds of the guelder-rose and of the currant and the sticky birch-buds were swollen with sap, and an exploring bee was humming about the golden blossoms that studded the willow. Larks trilled unseen above the velvety green fields and the ice-covered stubble-land; peewits wailed over the low lands and marshes flooded by the pools; cranes and wild geese flew high across the sky uttering their spring calls. The cattle, bald in patches where the new hair had not yet grown, lowed in the pastures; the bowlegged lambs frisked round their bleating mothers. Nimble children ran about the drying paths, covered with the prints of bare feet. There was a merry chatter of peasant women over their linen at the pond, and the ring of axes in the yard, where the peasants were repairing ploughs and harrows. The real spring had come.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Levin pulled on his big boots and, for the first time, a cloth jacket instead of his fur cloak, and went out to look after his farm, stepping over streams of water that flashed in the sunshine and dazzled his eyes, treading one moment on ice and the next into sticky mud.

Spring is the time for plans and projects. And as he came out into the farmyard, Levin, like a tree in spring that does not know what form will be taken by the young shoots and twigs imprisoned in its swelling buds, hardly knew what undertakings he was about to begin in the farm work that was so dear to him. But he felt that he was full of the most splendid plans and projects. First of all he went to the cattle. The cows had been let out into their paddock, and their smooth sides were already shining with their new, sleek spring coats; they basked in the sunshine and lowed to go to the meadow. Levin gazed admiringly at the cows he knew so intimately, down to the slightest detail of their condition, and gave orders for them to be driven out into the meadow, and for the calves to be let into the paddock. The herdsman ran off gaily to get ready for the meadow. The cowherd girls, picking up their petticoats, ran splashing through the mud with bare legs, still white, not yet brown from the sun, waving brushwood in their hands, chasing the calves that frolicked in the joy of spring.

After admiring the young ones of that year, who were particularly fine — the early calves were the size of a peasant's cow, and Pava's daughter, at three months, was as big as a yearling — Levin gave orders for a trough to be brought out and for them to be fed in the paddock. But it turned out that since the paddock had not been used during the winter, the hurdles made in the autumn for it had been broken. He sent for the carpenter, who, according to his orders, was supposed to be at work on the thrashing machine. But it turned out that the carpenter was repairing the harrows, which should have been repaired before Lent. This was very annoying to Levin. It was annoying to encounter that everlasting slovenliness in the farm work he had been fighting with all his might for so many years. The hurdles, as he learned, not being wanted in winter, had been carried to the cart-horses' stable, and there broken, since they were of light construction, only meant for feeding calves. Moreover, it was apparent too that the harrows and all the agricultural implements, which he had directed should be looked over and repaired in the winter — for which very purpose he had hired three carpenters — had not been put into repair, and the harrows were being repaired when they ought to have been harrowing the field. Levin sent for his bailiff, but immediately set off himself to look for him. The bailiff, beaming all over, like everyone that day, in a sheepskin bordered with astrachan, came out of the barn, twisting a bit of straw in his hands.
"Why isn't the carpenter at the thrashing machine?"
"Oh, I meant to tell you yesterday — the harrows need repairing. It's time they got to work in the fields."
"But what were they doing in the winter, then?"
"But what did you want the carpenter for?"
"Where are the hurdles for the calves' paddock?"
"I ordered them to be got ready. What can one do with peasants like these?" said the bailiff, waving a hand.

"It's not those peasants, it's this bailiff!" Levin said, getting angry. "Why, what do I keep you for?" he cried. But, realizing that this would not help matters, he stopped short in the middle of a sentence and merely sighed. "Well — can sowing begin?" he asked after a pause.
"Behind Turkin tomorrow or the day after they might begin."
"And the clover?"
"I've sent Vassily and Mishka — they're sowing. Only I don't know if they'll get through it; it's so slushy."
"How many acres?"
"About fifteen."
"Why not sow all of it?" Levin cried.

That they were only sowing clover on fifteen acres, not on all forty-five, was even more annoying to him. Clover, as he knew both from books and from his own experience, never did well unless it was sown as early as possible, almost in the snow. And yet Levin could never get this done.
"There's no one to send. What can one do with such a set of peasants? Three haven't turned up. And then there's Semyon..."
"Well, you should have taken some men off the thatching."
"That's what I have done."
"Where are the peasants, then?"
"Five are making compôte" (which meant compost), "four are shifting the oats for fear of a touch of mildew, Konstantin Dmitrievitch."
Levin knew very well that "a touch of mildew" meant his English seed oats were already ruined. Again they had not done as he had ordered.
"But I told you during Lent to put in pipes," he cried.
"Don't put yourself out — we'll get it all done in time."

Levin waved a hand angrily, went into the granary to glance at the oats, and then to the stable. The oats were not yet spoiled. But the peasants were carrying the oats with spades when they could have just let them slide down into the lower granary; and after arranging for this to be done, and taking two workmen from there for sowing clover, Levin got over his vexation with the bailiff. Indeed, it was such a lovely day that one could not be angry.
"Ignat!" he called to the coachman, who, with his sleeves rolled up, was washing the carriage wheels. "Saddle me..."
"Which one, sir?"
"Well, let it be Kolpik."
"Yes, sir."

While they were saddling his horse, Levin again called up the bailiff, who was hanging about in sight, to make peace with him, and began talking to him about the spring operations ahead and his plans for the farm.

The wagons were to begin carting manure earlier, so as to get it all done before the early mowing. And the ploughing of the further land was to go on without a break so as to let it ripen lying fallow. And the mowing was to be all done by hired labor, not on half-profits. The bailiff listened attentively, and obviously made an effort to approve his employer's projects. But he still had that look Levin knew so well, that always irritated him — a look of hopelessness and despondency. That look said: "That's all very well, but as God wills."

Nothing mortified Levin so much as that tone. But it was the tone common to all the bailiffs he had ever had. They had all taken up that attitude to his plans, so by now he was not angered by it, but mortified, and felt all the more roused to struggle against this seemingly elemental force continually ranged against him, for which he could find no other expression than "as God wills."
"If we can manage it, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the bailiff said.
"Why ever shouldn't you manage it?"
"We positively must have another fifteen laborers. And they don't turn up. There were some here today asking seventy roubles for the summer."

Levin was silent. Again he was face to face with that opposing force. He knew that however much they tried, they could not hire more than forty — perhaps thirty-seven or thirty-eight — laborers for a reasonable price. About forty had already been taken on, and there were no more. But still he could not help fighting against it.
"Send to Sury, to Tchefirovka; if they don't come we'll have to look for them."
"Oh, I'll send, to be sure," Vassily Fedorovitch said despondently. "But there are the horses too — they're not good for much."

"We'll get some more. I know, of course," Levin added, laughing, "you always want to make do with as little and as poor as possible; but this year I'm not going to let you have your way. I'll see to everything myself."
"Why, I don't think you take much rest as it is. It cheers us up to work under the master's eye..."
"So they're sowing clover behind the Birch Dale? I'll go and have a look at them," he said, getting on to the little bay cob, Kolpik, who was led up by the coachman.
"You can't get across the streams, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the coachman shouted.
"All right, I'll go by the forest."

And Levin rode through the slush of the farmyard out the gate and into the open country, his good little horse, after his long inactivity, stepping out gallantly, snorting over the pools, and asking, as it were, for guidance. If Levin had felt happy before in the cattle pens and farmyard, he felt happier still in the open country. Swaying rhythmically with the ambling paces of his good little cob, drinking in the warm yet fresh scent of the snow and the air, as he rode through his forest over the crumbling, wasted snow still left in patches, covered with dissolving tracks, he rejoiced over every tree, with the moss reviving on its bark and the buds swelling on its shoots. When he came out of the forest, in the immense plain before him his grass fields stretched in an unbroken carpet of green, without one bare place or swamp, only spotted here and there in the hollows with patches of melting snow. He was not put out of temper even by the sight of peasants' horses and colts trampling down his young grass (he told a peasant he met to drive them out), nor by the sarcastic and stupid reply of the peasant Ipat, whom he met on the way, and asked, "Well, Ipat, shall we soon be sowing?" "We must get the ploughing done first, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," Ipat answered. The further he rode, the happier he became, and plans for the land rose to his mind, each better than the last: to plant all his fields with hedges along the southern borders so the snow would not lie under them; to divide them up into six fields of arable and three of pasture and hay; to build a cattle yard at the further end of the estate, and to dig a pond, and to construct movable pens for the cattle as a means of manuring the land. And then eight hundred acres of wheat, three hundred of potatoes, and four hundred of clover, and not one acre exhausted.

Absorbed in such dreams, carefully keeping his horse by the hedges so as not to trample his young crops, he rode up to the laborers who had been sent to sow clover. A cart with the seed in it was standing, not at the edge, but in the middle of the crop, and the winter corn had been torn up by the wheels and trampled by the horse. Both laborers were sitting in the hedge, probably smoking a pipe together. The earth in the cart, with which the seed was mixed, was not crushed to powder, but crusted together or stuck in clods. Seeing the master, the laborer Vassily went toward the cart, while Mishka set to work sowing. This was not as it should be, but with the laborers Levin seldom lost his temper. When Vassily came up, Levin told him to lead the horse to the hedge.
"It's all right, sir, it'll spring up again," Vassily replied.
"Please don't argue," Levin said, "just do as you're told."

"Yes, sir," Vassily answered, and he took the horse's head. "What a sowing, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he said, hesitating; "first rate. Only it's a work to get about. You drag a ton of earth on your shoes."
"Why is it your earth isn't sifted?" Levin asked.
"Well, we crumble it up," Vassily answered, taking up some seed and rolling the earth in his palms.
Vassily was not to blame for their having filled his cart with unsifted earth, but still it was annoying.

Levin had more than once before tried a way he knew for stifling his anger and turning all that seemed dark right again, and he tried that way now. He watched how Mishka strode along, swinging the huge clods of earth that clung to each foot; and getting off his horse, he took the sieve from Vassily and started sowing himself.
"Where did you stop?"

Vassily pointed out the mark with his foot, and Levin set off as best he could, scattering seed across the land. Walking was as hard as on a bog, and by the time Levin had finished the row he was in a great heat, and he stopped and handed the sieve back to Vassily.
"Well, master, when summer's here, mind you don't scold me for these rows," said Vassily.
"Eh?" Levin said cheerily, already feeling the effect of his method.

"Why, you'll see come summertime. It'll look different. Look where I sowed last spring. How I did work at it! I do my best, Konstantin Dmitrievitch, you see, as I would for my own father. I don't like bad work myself, and I wouldn't let another man do it. What's good for the master's good for us too. To look out yonder now," Vassily said, pointing, "it does one's heart good."
"It's a lovely spring, Vassily."
"Why, it's a spring like the old men don't remember. I was up home; an old man up there has sown wheat too, about an acre of it. He said you wouldn't know it from rye."
"Have you been sowing wheat long?"
"Why, sir, you taught us the year before last. You gave me two measures. We sold about eight bushels and sowed a rood."
"Well, mind you crumble up the clods," Levin said, going toward his horse, "and keep an eye on Mishka. And if there's a good crop you shall have half a rouble for every acre."
"Humbly thankful. We are very well content, sir, as it is."
Levin got on his horse and rode toward the field with last year's clover, and the one ploughed ready for the spring corn.

The crop of clover coming up in the stubble was magnificent. It had survived everything, and stood up vividly green through the broken stalks of last year's wheat. The horse sank in up to the pasterns, and drew each hoof with a sucking sound out of the half-thawed ground. Over the ploughland riding was utterly impossible; the horse could only keep his footing where there was ice, and in the thawing furrows sank in deep at each step. The ploughland was in splendid condition; in a couple of days it would be fit for harrowing and sowing. Everything was capital, everything was cheering. Levin rode back across the streams, hoping the water would have gone down. And he did in fact get across, and startled two ducks. "There must be snipe too," he thought, and just as he reached the turning homeward he met the forest keeper, who confirmed his theory about the snipe.
Levin went home at a trot, so as to have time to eat his dinner and get his gun ready for the evening.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: As he rode up to the house in the happiest frame of mind, Levin heard the bell ring at the side of the main entrance.

"Yes, that's someone from the railway station," he thought, "just the right time to be here from the Moscow train... Who could it be? What if it's brother Nikolay? He did say: 'Maybe I'll go to the waters, or maybe I'll come down to you.'" He felt dismayed and vexed for the first minute that his brother Nikolay's presence should come and disturb his happy mood of spring. But he felt ashamed of the feeling, and at once opened, as it were, the arms of his soul, and with a softened feeling of joy and expectation, hoped now with all his heart that it was his brother. He pricked up his horse, and riding out from behind the acacias he saw a hired three-horse sledge from the railway station, and a gentleman in a fur coat. It was not his brother. "Oh, if only it were some nice person one could talk to a little!" he thought.
"Ah," Levin cried joyfully, flinging up both his hands. "Here's a delightful visitor! Ah, how glad I am to see you!" he shouted, recognizing Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"I'll find out for certain whether she's married, or when she's going to be married," he thought. And on that delicious spring day he felt that the thought of her did not hurt him at all.

"Well, you didn't expect me, eh?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, getting out of the sledge, splashed with mud on the bridge of his nose, on his cheek, on his eyebrows, but radiant with health and good spirits. "I've come to see you in the first place," he said, embracing and kissing him, "to have some stand-shooting second, and to sell the forest at Ergushovo third."
"Delightful! What a spring we're having! How ever did you get along in a sledge?"
"In a cart it would have been worse still, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," answered the driver, who knew him.
"Well, I'm very, very glad to see you," said Levin, with a genuine smile of childlike delight.

Levin led his friend to the room set apart for visitors, where Stepan Arkadyevitch's things were carried too — a bag, a gun in a case, a satchel for cigars. Leaving him there to wash and change his clothes, Levin went off to the counting house to speak about the ploughing and clover. Agafea Mihalovna, always very anxious for the credit of the house, met him in the hall with questions about dinner.
"Do just as you like, only let it be as soon as possible," he said, and went to the bailiff.
When he came back, Stepan Arkadyevitch, washed and combed, came out of his room with a beaming smile, and they went upstairs together.

"Well, I'm glad I managed to get away to you! Now I'll understand what the mysterious business is that you're always absorbed in here. No, really, I envy you. What a house, how nice it all is! So bright, so cheerful!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, forgetting that it was not always spring and fine weather like that day. "And your nurse is simply charming! A pretty maid in an apron might be even more agreeable, perhaps; but for your severe monastic style it does very well."
Stepan Arkadyevitch told him many interesting pieces of news; particularly interesting to Levin was the news that his brother, Sergey Ivanovitch, was planning to come visit him in the summer.

Not one word did Stepan Arkadyevitch say in reference to Kitty and the Shtcherbatskys; he merely gave him greetings from his wife. Levin was grateful to him for his delicacy and was very glad of his visitor. As always happened with him during his solitude, a mass of ideas and feelings had been accumulating within him that he could not share with those around him. And now he poured out upon Stepan Arkadyevitch his poetic joy in the spring, his failures and plans for the land, his thoughts and criticisms on the books he had been reading, and the idea of his own book, the basis of which was really, though he was unaware of it himself, a criticism of all the old books on agriculture. Stepan Arkadyevitch, always charming, understanding everything at the slightest hint, was particularly charming on this visit, and Levin noticed in him a special tenderness, as it were, and a new tone of respect that flattered him.

The efforts of Agafea Mihalovna and the cook to make the dinner particularly good only ended in the two famished friends attacking the preliminary course, eating a great deal of bread and butter, salt goose and salted mushrooms, and in Levin finally ordering the soup to be served without the accompaniment of little pies, with which the cook had particularly meant to impress their visitor. But though Stepan Arkadyevitch was accustomed to very different dinners, he thought everything excellent: the herb brandy, the bread, the butter, and above all the salt goose and the mushrooms, the nettle soup, the chicken in white sauce, the white Crimean wine — everything was superb and delicious.

"Splendid, splendid!" he said, lighting a fat cigar after the roast. "I feel as though, coming to you, I've landed on a peaceful shore after the noise and jolting of a steamer. And so you maintain that the laborer himself is an element to be studied and to regulate the choice of methods in agriculture. Of course, I'm an ignorant outsider; but I should imagine theory and its application will have its influence on the laborer too."

"Yes, but wait a bit. I'm not talking of political economy; I'm talking of the science of agriculture. It ought to be like the natural sciences, and observe given phenomena and the laborer in his economic, ethnographical..."
At that instant Agafea Mihalovna came in with jam.
"Oh, Agafea Mihalovna," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, kissing the tips of his plump fingers, "what salt goose, what herb brandy!... What do you think, isn't it time to start, Kostya?" he added.
Levin looked out the window at the sun sinking behind the bare treetops of the forest.
"Yes, it's time," he said. "Kouzma, get the trap ready," and he ran downstairs.

Stepan Arkadyevitch, going down, carefully took the canvas cover off his varnished gun case with his own hands, and opening it, began to get his expensive, new-fashioned gun ready. Kouzma, who already scented a big tip, never left Stepan Arkadyevitch's side, and put on him both his stockings and boots, a task Stepan Arkadyevitch readily let him do.
"Kostya, give orders that if the merchant Ryabinin comes... I told him to come today, he's to be shown in and asked to wait..."
"Why, do you mean to say you're selling the forest to Ryabinin?"
"Yes. Do you know him?"
"To be sure I do. I've had to do business with him, 'positively and conclusively.'"
Stepan Arkadyevitch laughed. "Positively and conclusively" were the merchant's favorite words.
"Yes, it's wonderfully funny how he talks. She knows where her master's going!" he added, patting Laska, who hung about Levin, whining and licking his hands, his boots, and his gun.
The trap was already at the steps when they went out.
"I told them to bring the trap round; or would you rather walk?"

"No, we'd better drive," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, getting into the trap. He sat down, tucked the tiger-skin rug round him, and lit a cigar. "How is it you don't smoke? A cigar is a sort of thing — not exactly a pleasure, but the crown and outward sign of pleasure. Come, this is life! How splendid it is! This is how I'd like to live!"
"Why, who's preventing you?" Levin said, smiling.
"No, you're a lucky man! You have everything you like. You like horses — you have them; dogs — you have them; shooting — you have it; farming — you have it."
"Perhaps because I rejoice in what I have and don't fret over what I haven't," Levin said, thinking of Kitty.
Stepan Arkadyevitch understood, looked at him, but said nothing.

Levin was grateful to Oblonsky for noticing, with his never-failing tact, that Levin dreaded conversation about the Shtcherbatskys, and so saying nothing about them. But now Levin was longing to find out what was tormenting him so much, yet he hadn't the courage to begin.
"Come, tell me how things are going with you," Levin said, remembering that it was not nice of him to think only of himself.
Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes sparkled merrily.

"You don't admit, I know, that one can be fond of new rolls when one has had one's rations of bread — to your mind it's a crime; but I don't count life as life without love," he said, taking Levin's question his own way. "What am I to do? I'm made that way. And really, one does so little harm to anyone, and gives oneself so much pleasure..."
"What! Is there something new, then?" Levin asked.

"Yes, my boy, there is! There, you see, you know the type of Ossian's women... Women, such as one sees in dreams... Well, these women are sometimes to be met in reality... and these women are terrible. Woman, don't you know, is such a subject that however much you study it, it's always perfectly new."
"Well, then, it would be better not to study it."
"No. Some mathematician has said that enjoyment lies in the search for truth, not in the finding it."
Levin listened in silence, and despite every effort, he could not in the least enter into his friend's feelings or understand his sentiments or the charm of studying such women.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The place chosen for the stand-shooting was not far above a stream in a little aspen copse. On reaching the copse, Levin got out of the trap and led Oblonsky to a corner of a mossy, swampy glade, already quite free of snow. He went back himself to a double birch on the other side, and, leaning his gun on the fork of a dead lower branch, took off his full overcoat, fastened his belt again, and worked his arms to see if they were free.

Gray old Laska, who had followed them, sat down warily opposite him and pricked up her ears. The sun was setting behind a thick forest, and in the glow of sunset the birches dotted about in the aspen copse stood out clearly with their hanging twigs and their buds swollen almost to bursting.

From the thickest parts of the copse, where the snow still remained, came the faint sound of thin, winding threads of water running away. Tiny birds twittered, and now and then fluttered from tree to tree.
In the pauses of complete stillness came the rustle of last year's leaves, stirred by the thawing of the earth and the growth of the grass.

"Imagine! One can hear and see the grass growing!" Levin said to himself, noticing a wet, slate-colored aspen leaf moving beside a blade of young grass. He stood, listened, and gazed sometimes down at the wet mossy ground, sometimes at Laska listening all alert, sometimes at the sea of bare tree tops stretching on the slope below him, sometimes at the darkening sky, covered with white streaks of cloud.

A hawk flew high over a distant forest with a slow sweep of its wings; another flew with exactly the same motion in the same direction and vanished. The birds twittered more and more loudly and busily in the thicket. An owl hooted not far off, and Laska, startling, stepped cautiously a few steps forward, and, putting her head on one side, began to listen intently. Beyond the stream the cuckoo was heard. Twice she uttered her usual cuckoo call, and then gave a hoarse, hurried call and broke down.
"Imagine — the cuckoo already!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, coming out from behind a bush.
"Yes, I hear it," Levin answered, reluctantly breaking the stillness with his voice, which sounded disagreeable to himself. "Now it's coming!"
Stepan Arkadyevitch's figure again disappeared behind the bush, and Levin saw nothing but the bright flash of a match, followed by the red glow and blue smoke of a cigarette.
"Tchk! tchk!" came the snapping sound of Stepan Arkadyevitch cocking his gun.
"What's that cry?" Oblonsky asked, drawing Levin's attention to a prolonged cry, as though a colt were whinnying in a high voice, in play.
"Oh, don't you know it? That's the hare. But enough talking! Listen — it's flying!" Levin almost shrieked, cocking his gun.

They heard a shrill whistle in the distance, and at exactly the time the sportsman knows so well, two seconds later — another, a third, and after the third whistle the hoarse, guttural cry could be heard.

Levin looked about him to the right and to the left, and there, just facing him against the dusky blue sky above the confused mass of tender aspen shoots, he saw the flying bird. It was flying straight toward him; the guttural cry, like the even tearing of some strong stuff, sounded close to his ear; the long beak and neck of the bird could be seen, and at the very instant Levin was taking aim, behind the bush where Oblonsky stood there was a flash of red lightning: the bird dropped like an arrow and darted upward again. Again came the red flash and the sound of a blow, and fluttering its wings as though trying to keep up in the air, the bird halted, stopped still an instant, and fell with a heavy splash on the slushy ground.
"Can I have missed it?" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted, who could not see for the smoke.

"Here it is!" Levin said, pointing to Laska, who, with one ear raised, wagging the end of her shaggy tail, came slowly back as though she would prolong the pleasure, and as it were smiling, brought the dead bird to her master. "Well, I'm glad you were successful," said Levin, who at the same time felt a touch of envy that he had not succeeded in shooting the snipe.
"It was a bad shot from the right barrel," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered, loading his gun. "Sh... it's flying!"

The shrill whistles rapidly following one another were heard again. Two snipe, playing and chasing each other, and only whistling, not crying, flew straight at the very heads of the sportsmen. There was the report of four shots, and like swallows the snipe turned swift somersaults in the air and vanished from sight.

The stand-shooting was capital. Stepan Arkadyevitch shot two more birds and Levin two, of which one was not found. It began to get dark. Venus, bright and silvery, shone with her soft light low down in the west behind the birch trees, and high up in the east twinkled the red lights of Arcturus. Over his head Levin made out the stars of the Great Bear and lost them again. The snipe had stopped flying; but Levin resolved to stay a little longer, till Venus, which he saw below a branch of birch, should be above it, and the stars of the Great Bear should be perfectly clear. Venus had risen above the branch, and the body of the Great Bear with its shaft was now all plainly visible against the dark blue sky, yet still he waited.
"Isn't it time to go home?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
It was quite still now in the copse, and not a bird was stirring.
"Let's stay a little while," Levin answered.
"As you like."
They were standing now about fifteen paces from one another.
"Stiva!" said Levin unexpectedly. "How is it you don't tell me whether your sister-in-law is married yet, or when she's going to be?"
Levin felt so resolute and serene that no answer, he fancied, could affect him. But he had never dreamed of what Stepan Arkadyevitch replied.
"She's never thought of getting married, and isn't thinking of it; but she's very ill, and the doctors have sent her abroad. They're positively afraid she may not live."
"What!" Levin cried. "Very ill? What's wrong with her? How has she...?"
While they were saying this, Laska, with ears pricked up, was looking upward at the sky, and reproachfully at them.
"They have chosen a time to talk," she was thinking. "It's on the wing... Here it is, yes, here it is. They'll miss it," thought Laska.

But at that very instant both suddenly heard a shrill whistle that, as it were, struck their ears, and both seized their guns at the same moment, and two flashes gleamed, and two bangs sounded in the very same instant. The snipe flying high above instantly folded its wings and fell into a thicket, bending down the delicate shoots.
"Splendid! Together!" Levin cried, and ran with Laska into the thicket to look for the snipe.
"Oh, yes — what was it that was unpleasant?" he wondered. "Yes, Kitty's ill... Well, it can't be helped; I'm very sorry," he thought.
"She's found it! Isn't she a clever thing?" he said, taking the warm bird from Laska's mouth and packing it into the almost full game bag. "I've got it, Stiva!" he shouted.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: On the way home Levin asked all the details of Kitty's illness and the Shtcherbatskys' plans, and though he would have been ashamed to admit it, he was pleased at what he heard. He was pleased that there was still hope, and still more pleased that she should be suffering who had made him suffer so much. But when Stepan Arkadyevitch began to speak of the causes of Kitty's illness and mentioned Vronsky's name, Levin cut him short.
"I have no right whatsoever to know about family matters, and, to tell the truth, no interest in them either."
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled almost imperceptibly, catching the instantaneous change he knew so well in Levin's face, which had become as gloomy as it had been bright a minute before.
"Have you quite settled it with Ryabinin about the forest?" Levin asked.
"Yes, it's settled. The price is magnificent: thirty-eight thousand. Eight straight away, and the rest in six years. I've been bothering about it forever. No one would offer more."
"Then you've as good as given away your forest for nothing," Levin said gloomily.
"How do you mean, for nothing?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch with a good-humored smile, knowing that nothing would be right in Levin's eyes now.
"Because the forest is worth at least a hundred and fifty roubles the acre," Levin answered.

"Oh, these farmers!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said playfully. "Your tone of contempt for us poor townsfolk!... But when it comes to business, we do it better than anyone. I assure you I've worked it all out," he said, "and the forest is fetching a very good price — so good that I'm afraid of this fellow's crying off, in fact. You know it's not 'timber,'" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, hoping by this distinction to convince Levin completely of the unfairness of his doubts. "And it won't run to more than twenty-five yards of fagots per acre, and he's giving me at the rate of seventy roubles the acre."

Levin smiled contemptuously. "I know," he thought, "that fashion — not only in him, but in all city people, who, after being twice in ten years in the country, pick up two or three phrases and use them in season and out of season, firmly convinced that they know all about it. '_Timber, run to so many yards the acre._' He uses those words without understanding them himself."

"I wouldn't try to teach you what you write about in your office," he said, "and if I needed to, I'd come to you to ask. But you're so positive you know all the lore of the forest. It's a hard thing. Have you counted the trees?"
"How count the trees?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, laughing, still trying to draw his friend out of his ill-temper. "Count the sands of the sea, number the stars. Some higher power might do it."

"Oh, well, the higher power of Ryabinin can. Not a single merchant ever buys a forest without counting the trees, unless they get it given them for nothing, the way you're doing now. I know your forest. I go there every year shooting, and your forest is worth a hundred and fifty roubles an acre paid down, while he's giving you sixty in installments. So you're in fact making him a present of thirty thousand."
"Come, don't let your imagination run away with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch piteously. "Why was it none would offer more, then?"

"Why, because he has an understanding with the merchants; he's bought them off. I've had to do with all of them; I know them. They're not merchants, you know — they're speculators. He wouldn't look at a bargain that gave him ten or fifteen percent profit, but holds back to buy a rouble's worth for twenty kopecks."
"Well, enough of it! You're out of temper."
"Not the least," said Levin gloomily, as they drove up to the house.

On the steps stood a trap tightly covered with iron and leather, with a sleek horse tightly harnessed in broad collar-straps. In the trap sat the chubby, tightly-belted clerk who served Ryabinin as coachman. Ryabinin himself was already in the house, and met the friends in the hall. Ryabinin was a tall, thinnish, middle-aged man, with mustache and a projecting clean-shaven chin, and prominent muddy-looking eyes. He wore a long-skirted blue coat with buttons below the waist at the back, and high boots wrinkled over the ankles and straight over the calf, with big galoshes drawn over them. He rubbed his face with his handkerchief, and wrapping his coat around him — though it already fit extremely well — he greeted them with a smile, holding out his hand to Stepan Arkadyevitch as though he wanted to catch hold of something.
"So here you are," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, giving him his hand. "That's capital."

"I did not venture to disregard your excellency's commands, though the road was extremely bad. I positively walked the whole way, but I am here on time. Konstantin Dmitrievitch, my respects," he turned to Levin, trying to seize his hand too. But Levin, scowling, made as though he did not see the hand, and took out the snipe. "Your honors have been diverting yourselves with the chase? What kind of bird might that be?" Ryabinin added, looking contemptuously at the snipe — "a great delicacy, I suppose." And he shook his head disapprovingly, as though he had grave doubts whether this game was worth the candle.
"Would you like to go into my study?" Levin said in French to Stepan Arkadyevitch, scowling morosely. "Go into my study; you can talk there."

"Quite so, wherever you please," Ryabinin said with contemptuous dignity, as though wishing to make it felt that others might be in difficulties about how to behave, but that he could never be in any difficulty about anything.

On entering the study Ryabinin looked about, as was his habit, as though seeking the holy picture, but when he had found it, he did not cross himself. He scanned the bookcases and bookshelves, and with the same dubious air with which he had regarded the snipe, he smiled contemptuously and shook his head disapprovingly, as though by no means willing to admit that this game was worth the candle.
"Well, have you brought the money?" Oblonsky asked. "Sit down."
"Oh, don't trouble yourself about the money. I've come to see you to talk it over."
"What is there to talk over? But do sit down."

"I don't mind if I do," Ryabinin said, sitting down and leaning his elbows on the back of his chair in a position of the most intense discomfort to himself. "You must knock it down a bit, prince. It would be too bad. The money is ready, down to the last farthing. As to paying the money down, there'll be no hitch there."
Levin, who had meanwhile been putting his gun away in the cupboard, was just on his way out the door, but on catching the merchant's words, he stopped.
"Why, you've got the forest for nothing as it is," he said. "He came to me too late, or I'd have fixed the price for him."
Ryabinin got up, and in silence, with a smile, looked Levin up and down.

"Very close about money is Konstantin Dmitrievitch," he said with a smile, turning to Stepan Arkadyevitch; "there's positively no dealing with him. I was bargaining for some wheat of his, and a pretty price I offered too."
"Why should I give you my goods for nothing? I didn't pick them up off the ground, nor steal them either."

"Mercy on us! Nowadays there's no chance at all of stealing. With the open courts and everything done in style, nowadays there's no question of stealing. We are just talking things over like gentlemen. His excellency's asking too much for the forest. I can't make both ends meet on it. I must ask for a little concession."
"But is the thing settled between you or not? If it's settled, it's useless haggling; but if it's not," Levin said, "I'll buy the forest."

The smile vanished from Ryabinin's face at once. A hawklike, greedy, cruel expression was left on it. With rapid, bony fingers he unbuttoned his coat, revealing a shirt, bronze waistcoat buttons, and a watch chain, and quickly pulled out a fat old pocketbook.

"Here you are, the forest is mine," he said, crossing himself quickly, and holding out his hand. "Take the money; it's my forest. That's Ryabinin's way of doing business; he doesn't haggle over every half-penny," he added, scowling and waving the pocketbook.
"I wouldn't be in a hurry if I were you," Levin said.
"Come, really," Oblonsky said in surprise. "I've given my word, you know."
Levin walked out of the room, slamming the door. Ryabinin looked toward the door and shook his head with a smile.

"It's all youthfulness — positively nothing but boyishness. Why, I'm buying it, upon my honor, simply, believe me, for the glory of it — that Ryabinin, and no one else, should have bought the copse of Oblonsky.
