She did not throw out all she had learned, but she had to admit she had deceived herself in thinking she could be what she had wanted to be. Her eyes were opened, as it were; she felt how hard it was to keep herself, free from hypocrisy and self-conceit, on the heights she had hoped to climb to. Beyond that, she felt the dreariness of the world of suffering, of sick and dying people, in which she had been moving. The effort she had been making to like it now seemed unbearable to her, and she longed to get back quickly into fresh air, to Russia, to Ergushovo, where, as she knew from letters, her sister Dolly had already gone with her children.
But her affection for Varenka didn't fade. Saying goodbye, Kitty begged her to come to them in Russia.
"I'll come when you get married," Varenka said.
"I shall never marry."
"Well, then, I shall never come."
"Well, then, I'll get married just for that. Now mind — remember your promise," Kitty said.
The doctor's prediction came true. Kitty went home to Russia cured. She was no longer as gay and thoughtless as before, but she was at peace. Her Moscow troubles had become a memory.
PART THREE

chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev wanted a rest from intellectual work, and instead of going abroad as he usually did, he came toward the end of May to stay in the country with his brother. In his judgment, country life was the best kind of life. He had come now to enjoy that life at his brother's. Konstantin Levin was very glad of his company, especially since he had not been expecting his brother Nikolay that summer. But for all his affection and respect for Sergey Ivanovitch, Konstantin Levin felt awkward with his brother in the country. He felt awkward, and even positively annoyed, by his brother's attitude toward country life. For Konstantin Levin the country was the ground of life itself — of its pleasures, its struggles, its labor. For Sergey Ivanovitch the country meant, on one hand, a rest from work, and on the other hand a valuable antidote to the corrupting influences of town, which he took with satisfaction and a sense of its usefulness. For Konstantin Levin the country was good first of all because it offered a field for labor whose usefulness was beyond question. For Sergey Ivanovitch the country was particularly fine because there one could, and was entitled to, do nothing. What was more, Sergey Ivanovitch's attitude toward the peasants got under Konstantin's skin. Sergey Ivanovitch was fond of saying he knew and liked the peasantry, and he often talked with peasants — which he knew how to do without affectation or condescension — and from every such conversation he would draw broad conclusions in favor of the peasantry and as proof that he understood them. Konstantin Levin did not like this kind of attitude toward the peasants. For Konstantin a peasant was simply the chief partner in their shared labor, and despite all the respect and the love — almost like kinship — he felt for the peasant (sucked in, as he said himself, with the milk of his peasant nurse), still, as a fellow worker, while he sometimes admired the strength, gentleness, and fairness of these men, he was just as often, when the work demanded other qualities, exasperated with the peasant for his carelessness, lack of method, drunkenness, and lying. If anyone had asked him whether he liked or disliked the peasants, Konstantin Levin would have been utterly at a loss for an answer. He liked them and didn't like them, just as he liked and didn't like men in general. Being a good-natured man, of course, he liked men more than he disliked them, and the same with the peasants. But to like or dislike "the people" as something separate he simply couldn't, not only because he lived with "the people" and all his interests were tied up with theirs, but also because he saw himself as part of "the people," couldn't see any special virtues or failings setting himself apart from them, and couldn't set himself against them. What was more, although he had lived in the closest contact with the peasants for years — as farmer, as arbitrator, and above all as adviser (the peasants trusted him, and for thirty miles around they would come to him for counsel) — he had no settled view of "the people," and would have been just as stumped to answer whether he knew "the people" as whether he liked them. For him to claim he knew the peasantry would have been the same as claiming to know men. He was constantly watching and getting to know people of all kinds, peasants among them, whom he saw as good and interesting people, and he was constantly finding new things in them, altering his old views of them and forming new ones. With Sergey Ivanovitch it was just the opposite. Just as he liked and praised country life by contrast with the life he didn't like, so he liked the peasantry by contrast with the class of men he didn't like, and so he knew the peasantry as something distinct from and opposed to men generally. In his methodical mind certain features of peasant life were sharply defined, deduced partly from peasant life itself but mostly from the contrast with other ways of life. He never changed his opinion of the peasantry or his sympathetic attitude toward them.

In the arguments that came up between the brothers about their views of the peasantry, Sergey Ivanovitch always got the better of his brother, precisely because Sergey Ivanovitch had a definite idea of the peasant — his character, his qualities, his tastes. Konstantin Levin had no fixed and unchanging view on the subject, so in their arguments Konstantin was easily caught contradicting himself.

In Sergey Ivanovitch's eyes his younger brother was a fine fellow, _with his heart in the right place_ (as he put it in French), but with a mind that, though quick enough, was too easily swayed by the impressions of the moment and so was full of contradictions. With all the condescension of an older brother he would sometimes explain to him what things really meant, but he got little satisfaction out of arguing with him, because the victories came too easily.

Konstantin Levin saw his brother as a man of immense intellect and culture, generous in the highest sense of the word, and gifted with a special capacity for work in the public good. But in the bottom of his heart, the older he grew and the more closely he knew his brother, the more often the thought struck him that this capacity for work in the public good — of which he felt himself entirely lacking — might not really be a quality at all, but a lack of something. Not a lack of good, honest, noble desires and tastes, but a lack of vital force, of what is called heart — the impulse that drives a man to choose one path out of all the countless paths of life and to care only about that one. The better he knew his brother, the more he noticed that Sergey Ivanovitch, and many of the others who worked for the public welfare, were not led by any impulse of the heart to care about the public good, but reasoned out from intellectual considerations that it was the right thing to take interest in public affairs, and so took interest in them. Levin was confirmed in this generalization by the fact that his brother took questions of the public welfare or of the immortality of the soul no more to heart than chess problems or the ingenious design of a new machine.

On top of all that, Konstantin Levin was not at ease with his brother because in summer in the country Levin was busy with farm work all the time, and the long summer day was not long enough for everything he had to do, while Sergey Ivanovitch was taking a holiday. But although he was on holiday now — that is, he was doing no writing — he was so used to intellectual activity that he liked to put the ideas that occurred to him into a clean, polished form, and liked to have someone to listen. His most usual and natural listener was his brother. So, despite the warmth and directness of their relations, Konstantin felt awkward leaving him alone. Sergey Ivanovitch liked to stretch out on the grass in the sun and lie there, basking and chatting lazily.
"You'd never believe," he would tell his brother, "how this rural idleness delights me. Not a thought in one's head — empty as a drum!"

But Konstantin Levin found it dull to sit and listen to him, especially when he knew that while he was away they would be carting dung onto fields that hadn't been ploughed for it, and piling it up any way they liked; that they wouldn't screw the shares into the ploughs, and would let them come off, and then say the new ploughs were a silly invention and nothing beat the old Andreevna plough, and so on.
"Come on — you've done enough tramping about in the heat," Sergey Ivanovitch would say to him.
"No, I just need to run round to the counting house for a minute," Levin would answer, and off he'd go to the fields.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Early in June it happened that Agafea Mihalovna, the old nurse and housekeeper, slipped while carrying a jar of mushrooms she had just pickled down to the cellar, fell, and sprained her wrist. The district doctor, a talkative young medical student who had just finished his training, came to see her. He examined the wrist, declared it wasn't broken, was delighted at the chance to talk with the famous Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev, and, to show off his progressive views, told him all the scandals of the district and complained of the wretched state the district council had fallen into. Sergey Ivanovitch listened attentively, asked questions, and, drawn out by a new listener, talked fluently, dropped a few sharp and weighty remarks, respectfully appreciated by the young doctor, and was soon in that eager state of mind his brother knew so well — the one that always came over him after a brilliant, animated conversation. After the doctor left, he wanted to take a fishing rod down to the river. Sergey Ivanovitch was fond of angling, and seemed almost proud of being able to take an interest in so foolish an occupation.
Konstantin Levin, whose presence was needed in the ploughland and the meadows, had come with the trap to pick his brother up.

It was that turning-point of summer when the year's crop is a certainty, when one starts thinking about the sowing for the next year, and the mowing is at hand; when the rye is all in ear, though the ears are still light and not yet full, and waves in gray-green billows in the wind; when the green oats, with tufts of yellow grass scattered through them here and there, droop unevenly over the late-sown fields; when the early buckwheat is already out and hiding the ground; when the fallow lands, beaten hard as stone by the cattle, are half ploughed up with paths still untouched by the plough; when from the dry dung heaps carted out onto the fields at sunset comes a smell of manure mixed with meadowsweet; and when down in the lowlands the riverside meadows are a thick sea of grass waiting to be mown, with blackened heaps of sorrel stalks scattered through it.

It was that brief lull in the work of the fields, just before the start of the harvest labors — labors that come round year after year, year after year stretching every nerve of the peasants. The crop was splendid, and bright hot summer days had set in, with short, dewy nights.

The brothers had to drive through the woods to reach the meadows. Sergey Ivanovitch was admiring the beauty of the woods the whole way — a tangled mass of leaves — pointing out to his brother now an old lime tree about to flower, dark on its shady side and brightly speckled with yellow stipules, now the year's young saplings brilliant with emerald. Konstantin Levin did not enjoy talking or hearing about the beauty of nature. Words, for him, drained the beauty out of what he saw. He agreed with what his brother said, but he could not help his thoughts drifting to other matters. When they came out of the woods, his attention was caught entirely by the view of the fallow on the upland, yellow in places with grass, in places trampled and seamed with furrows, in places dotted with ridges of dung, in places already ploughed. A string of carts was moving across it. Levin counted the carts and was pleased to see that all the carts he needed had been brought, and at the sight of the meadows his thoughts turned to the mowing. There was always something about haymaking that touched him to the quick. When they reached the meadow, Levin stopped the horse.

The morning dew was still lying on the thick undergrowth of grass, and so that he wouldn't get his feet wet, Sergey Ivanovitch asked his brother to drive him in the trap up to the willow from which carp were caught. As sorry as Konstantin Levin was to crush down his own mowing grass, he drove him into the meadow. The high grass turned softly around the wheels and the horse's legs, leaving its seeds clinging to the wet axles and spokes. His brother settled himself under a bush, sorting out his tackle, while Levin led the horse away, fastened him up, and walked into the vast gray-green sea of grass, motionless in the windless air. The silky grass, with its ripe seed, came almost up to his waist in the wettest spots.
Crossing the meadow, Konstantin Levin came out onto the road and met an old man with a swollen eye, carrying a skep on his shoulder.
"What, picked up a stray swarm, Fomitch?" he asked.

"No, indeed, Konstantin Dmitrich! All we can do to hold onto our own! This is the second swarm that's flown away. Lucky the lads caught them. They were ploughing your field. They unyoked the horses and tore after them."
"Well, what do you say, Fomitch — start the mowing, or wait a bit?"
"Eh, well. Our way is to wait till St. Peter's Day. But you always mow earlier. Well, sure enough, please God, the hay is good. There'll be plenty for the beasts."
"What do you think about the weather?"
"That's in God's hands. Maybe it'll hold fine."
Levin went over to his brother.

Sergey Ivanovitch had caught nothing, but he wasn't bored, and seemed in the cheerfullest of moods. Levin could see that, fired up by his talk with the doctor, he wanted to talk on. Levin himself, on the other hand, would have liked to get home as quickly as possible, so as to give the orders for gathering the mowers for the next day and to settle the doubts about the mowing that were eating at him.
"Well, let's be off," he said.

"Why be in such a rush? Let's stay a bit. But look how wet you are! Even if you catch nothing, it's still pleasant. That's the best thing about every kind of sport — that one is dealing with nature. Look at this steely water — how lovely it is!" said Sergey Ivanovitch. "These riverbanks always remind me of the riddle — do you know it? 'The grass says to the water: we shiver and we shiver.'"
"I don't know the riddle," Levin answered wearily.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: "Do you know, I've been thinking about you," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "What's going on in the district is beyond anything, judging by what this doctor tells me. He's a very intelligent fellow. And as I've told you before, I tell you again: it's not right that you don't go to the meetings, that you keep out of the district business altogether. If decent men won't get involved, of course the whole thing goes wrong. We pay the money, and it all goes in salaries, and there are no schools, no district nurses, no midwives, no drugstores — nothing."
"Well, I tried, you know," Levin said slowly and unwillingly. "I can't! And there's nothing to be done about it."
"But why can't you? I'll be honest, I don't get it. Indifference, incapacity — I won't accept; surely it's not just laziness?"
"None of those things. I tried, and I see I can do nothing," Levin said.

He had barely been following what his brother was saying. Looking off toward the ploughland across the river, he could make out something black, but he could not tell whether it was a horse or the bailiff on horseback.
"Why is it you can do nothing? You made an attempt, didn't succeed — as you put it — and you give up. How can you have so little self-respect?"

"Self-respect!" said Levin, stung by his brother's words. "I don't understand. If at college they'd told me other people understood the integral calculus and I didn't, then pride would have come into it. But in this case you have to be convinced first that you have certain qualifications for this sort of work, and above all that the whole business is of great importance."

"What — do you mean to say it's not of importance?" said Sergey Ivanovitch, stung in his turn that his brother should call anything he cared about unimportant, and even more that he was so clearly paying little attention to what was being said.

"I don't think it's important; it doesn't grip me, I can't help that," Levin answered, making out that the figure was the bailiff, and that the bailiff seemed to be letting the peasants off the ploughed land. They were turning the plough over. "Could they really have finished ploughing already?" he wondered.

"Now really," said the elder brother, a crease in his handsome, clever face, "there are limits to everything. It's all very well to be original and genuine and to dislike whatever's conventional — I know all about that; but really, what you're saying either has no meaning or has a very wrong meaning. How can you think it of no importance whether the peasant, whom you love as you say —"
"I never said any such thing," Konstantin Levin thought.

"— dies without help? The ignorant peasant-women starve the children, the people stagnate in darkness and are helpless in the hands of every village clerk, while you have at your disposal a way of helping them, and don't help them because, in your mind, it's not important."
And Sergey Ivanovitch laid out the alternative: either you are so undeveloped that you can't see all you could do, or you won't sacrifice your ease, your vanity, or whatever it is, to do it.
Konstantin Levin felt there was no way out for him except to submit, or to admit to a lack of zeal for the public good. And that mortified him and hurt his feelings.
"It's both," he said firmly: "I don't see that it was possible —"
"What! Was it impossible, if the money were properly spent, to provide medical aid?"

"Impossible, as far as I can see. With the three thousand square miles of our district, with our thaws, and the storms, and the work in the fields, I don't see how medical care could be provided everywhere. And on top of that, I don't believe in medicine."
"Oh, come, that's unfair — I could quote you thousands of cases. But the schools, anyway."
"Why schools?"
"What do you mean? Is there any question that education is a good thing? If it's good for you, it's good for everyone."
Konstantin Levin felt himself morally pinned to a wall, and so he grew hot and blurted out, without thinking, the real reason for his indifference to public affairs.

"Perhaps it may all be very fine; but why should I bother myself setting up dispensaries I'll never use, and schools I'll never send my children to, that even the peasants don't want to send their children to, and that I'm not at all sure they ought to send them to?" he said.

Sergey Ivanovitch was for a moment thrown by this unexpected angle on the question; but he quickly worked out a new line of attack. He sat in silence for a little, drew out his hook, threw it back in, and turned to his brother with a smile.
"Now come — in the first place, the dispensary is needed. We ourselves sent for the district doctor for Agafea Mihalovna."
"Oh, well — I have a feeling her wrist will never be straight again."
"That remains to be seen. Next, the peasant who can read and write is a more useful, more valuable worker to you."

"No, ask anyone you like," Konstantin Levin answered firmly. "A man who can read and write is much worse as a worker. And mending the highroads is impossible; and the moment they put up a bridge, it gets stolen."

"Still, that's not the point," said Sergey Ivanovitch, frowning. He disliked being contradicted, and disliked even more arguments that kept jumping from one thing to another, throwing in new and unrelated points, so that there was no telling which one to answer. "Do you grant that education is a good thing for the people?"

"Yes, I grant it," Levin said without thinking, and at once felt he had said what he didn't mean. He saw that if he granted that, it would be proved he had been talking meaningless rubbish. How exactly it would be proved he didn't know, but he knew it would inevitably be proved to him by logic, and he braced himself for the proofs.
The argument turned out to be far simpler than he expected.
"If you grant that it is a good thing," Sergey Ivanovitch said, "then, as an honest man, you can't help caring about it and sympathizing with the movement, and therefore wanting to work for it."
"But I still don't grant that this movement is just," said Konstantin Levin, reddening a little.
"What! But you just said —"
"That is, I don't grant that it's either good or feasible."
"That you can't tell without making the trial."
"Well, suppose that's so," Levin said, though he did not at all suppose so, "suppose that's so — still, I don't see why I'm to bother myself with it."
"How so?"
"No — since we're at it, explain it to me from the philosophical point of view," Levin said.
"I don't see where philosophy comes in," Sergey Ivanovitch said, in a tone that struck Levin as not granting his brother the right to talk philosophy. And that annoyed Levin.

"I'll tell you, then," he said heatedly. "I think the mainspring of all our actions is, after all, self-interest. Now, in our local institutions, I, as a nobleman, see nothing that helps my prosperity, and the roads are not better and could not be better; my horses carry me well enough over bad ones. I have no use for doctors and dispensaries. I have no use for an arbitrator of disputes — I never appeal to him and never will. The schools are no good to me — they're actually harmful, as I've told you. For me the district institutions simply mean having to pay fourpence-halfpenny per three acres, drive into town, sleep with the bugs, and listen to all kinds of stupidity and vileness, and self-interest offers me no reason to do any of it."
"Excuse me," Sergey Ivanovitch broke in with a smile, "self-interest didn't push us to work for the emancipation of the serfs, but we worked for it."

"No!" Konstantin Levin cut in with still more heat. "The emancipation of the serfs was another matter. There, self-interest came in. We longed to throw off that yoke that crushed all decent people among us. But to be a town councilor and debate how many dustmen are needed, and how chimneys are to be built in a town I don't live in — to serve on a jury and try a peasant who's stolen a flitch of bacon, and sit for six hours straight listening to all kinds of jabber from defense and prosecution counsel, and the president cross-examining my old half-witted Alioshka, 'Do you admit, prisoner in the dock, the fact of the removal of the bacon?' 'Eh?'"
Konstantin Levin had warmed to his theme and was now imitating the president and the half-witted Alioshka: it seemed to him perfectly to the point.
But Sergey Ivanovitch shrugged.
"Well, what is it you mean to say, then?"

"I simply mean that the rights that touch me — my interest — I'll always defend as best I can; that when they raided us students and the police read our letters, I was ready to defend those rights to the utmost, to defend my rights to education and freedom. I can understand compulsory military service, which affects my children, my brothers, and myself; I'm ready to deliberate on what concerns me; but deliberating on how to spend forty thousand roubles of district council money, or on judging the half-witted Alioshka — I don't understand and I can't do it."
Konstantin Levin was speaking as if the floodgates of his speech had burst open. Sergey Ivanovitch smiled.
"But tomorrow it'll be your turn to be tried — would it have suited your tastes better to be tried in the old criminal court?"

"I'm not going to be tried. I'm not going to murder anyone, and I have no need of it. Well, I'll tell you what," he went on, flying off again onto a subject entirely beside the point, "our district self-government and all the rest of it — it's just like the birch branches we stick in the ground on Trinity Day to make it look like a copse that's grown up of itself in Europe, and I can't enthuse over these birch branches or believe in them."
Sergey Ivanovitch merely shrugged, as if to mark his surprise at how the birch branches had wandered into the argument at this point — though in fact he understood at once what his brother meant.
"Excuse me, but you really can't argue that way," he observed.
But Konstantin Levin wanted to justify himself for the failing he was aware of — his lack of zeal for the public welfare — and he kept going.

"I think," he said, "that no kind of activity is likely to last if it isn't grounded in self-interest. That's a universal principle, a philosophical principle," he said, repeating the word "philosophical" with emphasis, as if to show he had as much right to talk philosophy as anyone else.
Sergey Ivanovitch smiled. "He too has a philosophy of his own, ready to serve his natural inclinations," he thought.

"Come, you'd better leave philosophy alone," he said. "The central problem of the philosophy of every age is precisely the necessary connection between individual and social interest. But never mind that; what does matter is a correction I have to make in your comparison. The birches aren't simply stuck in; some are sown and some are planted, and one has to treat them with care. It's only those peoples that have an intuitive sense of what matters and what counts in their institutions, and know how to value them, that have a future before them — those are the only peoples one can truly call historical."
And Sergey Ivanovitch carried the discussion off into the regions of philosophical history, where Konstantin Levin could not follow him, and showed him at full length the wrongness of his view.
"As for your dislike of it, forgive me for saying so, that's simply our Russian sloth and old serf-owner's habits, and I'm sure that in you it's a passing error and will go."

Konstantin said nothing. He felt himself beaten on every side, but he also felt that what he wanted to say could not be made plain to his brother. Only he could not decide whether it was unintelligible because he wasn't capable of putting his meaning clearly, or because his brother would not or could not understand him. But he didn't pursue that thought, and without replying he fell to thinking about a quite different, personal matter.
Sergey Ivanovitch wound up the last line, untied the horse, and they drove off.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: The personal matter that had absorbed Levin during his conversation with his brother was this. Once, a year or two earlier, he had gone to look at the mowing, and made very angry by the bailiff, he had reached for his favorite means of regaining his temper — he had taken a scythe from a peasant and started mowing himself.

He had liked the work so much that he had tried his hand at mowing a number of times since. He had cut the whole meadow in front of his house, and ever since the early spring of this year he had been turning over the idea of mowing for entire days alongside the peasants. Since his brother's arrival he had been in two minds about it. He didn't like the thought of leaving his brother alone all day long, and he was afraid his brother would laugh at him about it. But as he drove into the meadow and remembered what mowing felt like, he very nearly made up his mind that he would go. After the irritating argument with his brother, he thought about that intention again.
"I need physical exercise — without it my temper is bound to be ruined," he thought, and he resolved to go mowing, however awkward it might be with his brother or with the peasants.

Toward evening Konstantin Levin walked over to his counting house, gave orders for the next day's work, and sent word round the village to gather the mowers for the morrow, to cut Kalinov Meadow, the largest and best of his grasslands.
"And please send my scythe over to Tit, for him to set, and have it brought back tomorrow. I may do some mowing myself," he said, trying not to sound embarrassed.
The bailiff smiled and said, "Yes, sir."
Over tea that evening, Levin said to his brother:
"I think the fine weather will hold. Tomorrow I'll start mowing."
"I'm very fond of that kind of fieldwork," said Sergey Ivanovitch.
"I love it. I sometimes mow with the peasants myself, and tomorrow I want to try mowing the whole day."
Sergey Ivanovitch lifted his head and looked at his brother with interest.
"How do you mean? Just like one of the peasants — all day long?"
"Yes, it's very pleasant," Levin said.
"It's splendid as exercise, only you'll hardly be able to stand it," Sergey Ivanovitch said, without a trace of irony.
"I've tried it. It's hard going at first, but you get into it. I think I'll be able to keep it up."
"Really? What an idea! But tell me — how do the peasants take it? I imagine they have a quiet laugh at the master's being such an odd fish?"
"No, I don't think so; but the work is so satisfying and so demanding at once, that there's no time to think about it."
"But how will you manage about dinner with them? It would be a bit awkward to send you out a bottle of Lafitte and a roast turkey."
"No, I'll just come back home at the time of their noonday rest."
Next morning Konstantin Levin got up earlier than usual, but he was held up giving directions on the farm, and by the time he reached the mowing the men were already on their second row.

From the higher ground he could see the shaded, cut stretch of meadow below, with its grayish ridges of cut grass, and the black heaps of coats the mowers had taken off at the spot where they had started cutting.

Bit by bit, as he rode toward the meadow, the peasants came into sight — some in coats, some in their shirts — mowing one behind another in a long line, swinging their scythes each in his own rhythm. He counted forty-two of them.

They were moving slowly across the uneven low-lying part of the meadow, where there had once been an old dam. Levin recognized some of his own men. There was old Yermil in a very long white smock, bent forward as he swung his scythe; there was Vaska, a young fellow who had been a coachman of Levin's, taking each row with a wide sweep. And there was Tit, Levin's master in the art of mowing — a thin little peasant. He was out ahead of them all, cutting his wide row without stooping, as if he were playing with the scythe.
Levin got down from his mare, tied her up by the roadside, and went to meet Tit, who pulled out a second scythe from a bush and handed it to him.
"It's ready, sir; like a razor, cuts of itself," Tit said, taking off his cap with a smile and giving him the scythe.

Levin took the scythe and began testing it. As they finished their rows, the mowers, hot and good-humored, came out onto the road one after another, laughing a little and greeting the master. They all stared at him, but no one said anything, until a tall old man with a wrinkled, beardless face, in a short sheepskin jacket, stepped out onto the road and spoke to him.
"Now then, master — once you take hold of the rope there's no letting go!" he said, and Levin heard smothered laughter among the mowers.
"I'll try not to let go," he said, taking his place behind Tit and waiting for the moment to start.
"Mind yourself," the old man repeated.

Tit made room, and Levin started off behind him. The grass was short close to the road, and Levin, who had not mowed for a long time and was thrown off by the eyes fixed on him, cut badly the first few moments, although he was swinging the scythe vigorously. Behind him he heard voices:
"It's not set right; the handle's too high; look at the way he has to stoop to it," said one.
"Bear more on the heel," said another.
"Never mind, he'll get on all right," the old man put in.

"He's made a start. You're swinging too wide, you'll wear yourself out. The master, sure, does his best for himself! But look at the grass missed there! For work like that the rest of us would catch it!"

The grass turned softer, and Levin, listening without answering, followed Tit, trying to do the best he could. They covered a hundred paces. Tit kept moving on, not stopping, not showing the slightest weariness, but Levin was already starting to worry that he wouldn't be able to keep it up: he was so tired.

He felt, as he swung his scythe, that he was at the very end of his strength, and he was on the point of asking Tit to stop. At that very moment Tit stopped of his own accord, bent down, picked up some grass, rubbed his scythe with it, and began whetting it. Levin straightened up, drew a deep breath, and looked around. Behind him a peasant came along, and he too was clearly tired, because he stopped at once without waiting to mow up to Levin and began whetting his scythe. Tit sharpened his own scythe and Levin's, and they went on. Next time it was the same. Tit moved on with sweep after sweep, not stopping or showing any sign of weariness. Levin followed him, trying not to fall behind, and finding it harder and harder; the moment came when he felt he had no strength left, and just then Tit stopped and whetted the scythes.

So they got through the first row. And this long row felt particularly hard to Levin; but when the end was reached and Tit, scythe on shoulder, started back at a deliberate stride over the tracks his heels had left in the cut grass, and Levin walked back in the same way along the strip he had just mown, in spite of the sweat that streamed down his face and dripped from his nose and soaked his back as though he'd been dunked in water, he felt very happy. What pleased him most was that he knew now he would be able to hold out.

His pleasure was only spoiled by the fact that his row was not well cut. "I'll swing less with my arm and more with my whole body," he thought, comparing Tit's row — which looked as if it had been laid out with a line — with his own, which lay unevenly and crookedly.

Levin had noticed that Tit had mowed the first row especially fast, probably to test his master, and the row happened to be a long one. The next rows were easier, but Levin still had to strain every nerve not to fall behind the peasants.

He thought of nothing, wanted nothing, except not to be left behind the peasants and to do his work as well as he could. He heard nothing but the swish of scythes, and he saw before him Tit's upright figure mowing on ahead, the crescent-shaped curve of the cut grass, the grass and flower heads falling slowly and rhythmically before the blade of his scythe, and ahead of him the end of the row, where the rest would come.

Suddenly, in the middle of his toil, without understanding what it was or where it came from, he felt a pleasant coolness on his hot, damp shoulders. He glanced at the sky during the next pause for whetting. A heavy, low storm cloud had blown up, and big drops of rain were falling. Some of the peasants went over to their coats and put them on; others — like Levin himself — just shrugged their shoulders, enjoying the cool of it.

Another row, and yet another row, followed — long rows and short rows, with good grass and with poor grass. Levin lost all sense of time and could not have said whether it was late or early now. A change began to come over his work, which gave him immense satisfaction. In the middle of his labor came moments when he forgot what he was doing, and it all came easy, and at those same moments his row was almost as smooth and well cut as Tit's. But as soon as he remembered what he was doing and began trying to do better, he was at once aware of all the difficulty of the task, and the row was poorly mown.

He had finished yet another row and would have gone back to the top of the meadow to begin the next, but Tit stopped, went up to the old man, and said something to him in a low voice. They both looked at the sun. "What are they talking about, and why doesn't he go back?" Levin wondered, not realizing that the peasants had been mowing for no less than four hours without a break, and that it was time for their lunch.
"Lunch, sir," the old man said.
"Is it really time? All right, then — lunch."

Levin handed his scythe back to Tit and, with the peasants — who were crossing the long stretch of mown grass, lightly sprinkled with rain, to get their bread from the heap of coats — he set off toward his house. Only then did he suddenly realize he had been wrong about the weather, and that the rain was drenching his hay.
"The hay will be spoiled," he said.
"Not a bit of it, sir; mow in the rain, and you'll rake in fine weather!" the old man said.

Levin untied his horse and rode home to his coffee. Sergey Ivanovitch was only just getting up. By the time he had drunk his coffee, Levin was riding back to the mowing before Sergey Ivanovitch had had time to dress and come down to the dining room.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: After lunch Levin was no longer in the same place in the line of mowers as before; he stood between the old man who had teased him earlier, and who now invited him to be his neighbor, and a young peasant who had only been married in the autumn and who was mowing this summer for the first time.

The old man, holding himself erect, moved at the front, his feet turned outward, taking long, even strides, and with a steady, precise motion that seemed to cost him no more effort than swinging one's arms in walking — as if it were a game — he laid down the tall, even row of grass. It was as if the sharp scythe itself, and not he, were swishing through the juicy grass.

Behind Levin came the lad Mishka. His pretty boyish face, with a twist of fresh grass bound around his hair, was straining hard with the effort; but whenever anyone looked at him, he smiled. He would clearly have died sooner than admit the work was hard for him.

Levin kept between them. In the worst of the day's heat the mowing did not seem so hard to him. The sweat he was drenched in cooled him, and the sun beating on his back, his head, and his arms — bare to the elbow — gave a vigor and a stubborn drive to his labor; and more and more often came those moments of unconsciousness when one could stop thinking about what one was doing. The scythe cut by itself. These were the happy moments. More delightful still were the moments when they reached the stream where the rows ended, and the old man wiped his scythe with the wet, thick grass, rinsed the blade in the fresh water of the stream, dipped out a little water in a tin dipper, and offered Levin a drink.
"What do you say to my home-brew, eh? Good, eh?" he said with a wink.

And truly Levin had never drunk any drink as good as this warm water with bits of green floating in it and a taste of rust from the tin dipper. And right after this came the delicious slow saunter back, hand on the scythe, during which he could wipe away the streaming sweat, draw deep breaths of air, and look around at the long line of mowers and at what was happening in the forest and the countryside.

The longer Levin mowed, the more often the moments of unconsciousness came over him, in which it seemed not his hands swinging the scythe, but the scythe itself doing the mowing — a body full of life and consciousness of its own — and as if by magic, without his thinking about it, the work turned out regular and well-finished on its own. These were the most blissful moments.

It was hard work only when he had to break off the motion that had become unconscious and start thinking again; when he had to mow round a hillock or a tuft of sorrel. The old man did this easily. Whenever a hillock came he changed his action, and at one moment with the heel and at another with the tip of the scythe, he clipped the hillock round both sides with short strokes. And while he did this he kept looking around and watching everything in view: at one moment he would pick a wild berry and eat it or hold it out to Levin, then he would flick away a twig with the blade of the scythe, then he would look at a quail's nest from which the bird flew up right under his scythe, or catch a snake that crossed his path and, lifting it on the scythe as if on a fork, show it to Levin and fling it aside.

For both Levin and the young peasant behind him, such changes of position were difficult. Both of them, repeating one strained movement over and over again, were in a kind of frenzy of toil and were incapable of shifting their position while watching what lay before them.

Levin had no sense of how time was passing. If asked how long he had been working, he would have said half an hour — and it was getting on for dinner time. As they were walking back over the cut grass, the old man drew Levin's attention to the little girls and boys coming from various directions, barely visible through the tall grass, and along the road toward the mowers, lugging sacks of bread that dragged at their little hands, and pitchers of sour rye beer with cloths wrapped around them.
"Look'ee, the little ants crawling!" he said, pointing to them, and he shaded his eyes with his hand to look at the sun. They mowed two more rows; the old man stopped.

"Come, master — dinner time!" he said briskly. And when they reached the stream the mowers crossed the lines of cut grass over to their pile of coats, where the children who had brought their dinners were sitting waiting. The peasants gathered into groups — those further away under a cart, those closer in under a willow bush.
Levin sat down by them; he had no wish to leave.

All shyness with the master had long since gone. The peasants got ready for dinner. Some washed, the young lads bathed in the stream, others fixed themselves a comfortable spot to rest, untied their bread sacks, and uncovered the jugs of rye beer. The old man crumbled some bread into a cup, stirred it with the handle of a spoon, poured water on it from the dipper, broke up some more bread, salted it, and then turned to the east to say his prayer.
"Come, master — try my sop," he said, kneeling down before the cup.

The sop was so good that Levin gave up the idea of going home. He had his meal with the old man, talked with him about his family matters, took the keenest interest in them, and told him about his own affairs and any details of his life that might interest the old man. He felt himself closer to him than to his own brother, and could not help smiling at the affection he felt for this man. When the old man got up again, said his prayer, and lay down under a bush, putting some grass under his head for a pillow, Levin did the same; and in spite of the clinging flies that were so persistent in the sun, and the midges that tickled his hot face and body, he fell asleep at once and only woke when the sun had moved to the other side of the bush and was reaching him. The old man had been awake a long time and was sitting up, whetting the scythes of the younger lads.

Levin looked around and hardly recognized the place, everything was so changed. The huge stretch of meadow had been mown and was sparkling with a peculiar fresh brilliance, its rows of already sweet-smelling grass laid out in the slanting evening sun. The bushes around the river had been cut down, the river itself, hidden before, was now gleaming like steel in its bends, and the moving, rising line of peasants, and the sharp wall of grass of the unmown part of the meadow, and the hawks hovering over the stripped meadow — all of it was perfectly new. Raising himself, Levin began calculating how much had been cut and how much more could still be done that day.

The work done was uncommonly large for forty-two men. They had cut the whole of the big meadow, which back in the days of serf labor had taken thirty scythes two days to mow. Only the corners were left, where the rows were short. But Levin felt a longing to get as much mown that day as possible, and was vexed that the sun was sinking so quickly. He felt no weariness at all; he only wanted to get the work done more and more quickly, and as much of it as possible.
"Could you cut Mashkin Upland too, do you think?" he said to the old man.
"As God wills — the sun's not high yet. A little vodka for the lads?"
At the afternoon rest, when they were sitting down again and those who smoked had lit their pipes, the old man told the men that "Mashkin Upland's to be cut — there'll be some vodka."
"Why not cut it? Come on, Tit! We'll look sharp! We can eat at night. Come on!" voices cried, and finishing off their bread, the mowers went back to work.
"Come, lads, keep it up!" Tit said, and ran on ahead at almost a trot.
"Get along, get along!" the old man said, hurrying after him and easily overtaking him. "I'll mow you down, look out!"

And young and old mowed away as if racing one another. But for all their speed, they did not spoil the grass, and the rows were laid down just as neatly and exactly as before. The little patch left uncut in the corner was mown in five minutes. The last of the mowers were just finishing their rows while the first ones flung their coats over their shoulders and crossed the road toward Mashkin Upland.

The sun was already sinking into the trees when, with their jingling dippers, they entered the wooded ravine of Mashkin Upland. The grass was waist-high in the middle of the hollow, soft, tender, and feathery, dotted here and there among the trees with wild heart's-ease.

After a brief consultation — whether to take the rows lengthwise or diagonally — Prohor Yermilin, another famous mower, a huge, black-haired peasant, went on ahead. He climbed to the top, turned back, and started mowing, and all the others fell in behind him, going downhill through the hollow and uphill right up to the edge of the forest. The sun sank behind the trees. The dew was falling now; the mowers were in the sun only on the hillside, but below, where a mist was rising, and on the opposite slope, they mowed into fresh, dewy shadow. The work went on quickly. The grass cut with a juicy sound and was at once laid in high, fragrant rows. The mowers from every side, drawn close together in the short row, kept urging each other on with jingling dippers and clanging scythes and the hiss of whetstones sharpening them, and with good-humored shouts.

Levin still kept between the young peasant and the old man. The old man, who had put on his short sheepskin jacket, was just as good-humored, just as full of jokes, just as free in his movements as before. Among the trees they kept cutting with their scythes the so-called "birch mushrooms," swollen fat in the lush grass. But every time the old man came across a mushroom he bent down, picked it up, and tucked it into his shirt. "Another present for my old woman," he said as he did so.

Easy as it was to mow the wet, soft grass, it was hard work going up and down the steep sides of the ravine. But it didn't trouble the old man. Swinging his scythe just as ever, taking firm little steps with his feet in their big plaited shoes, he climbed slowly up the steep stretch, and although his breeches hung out below his smock and his whole frame shook with effort, he didn't miss a single blade of grass or a single mushroom along the way, and went on cracking jokes with the peasants and with Levin. Levin walked behind him and kept thinking he was bound to fall, as he climbed with a scythe up a steep face where it would have been hard work to climb without anything in your hands. But up he went, and did what he had to do. He felt as if some external force were carrying him along.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Mashkin Upland was mown, the last row finished, the peasants had put on their coats and were gaily trudging home. Levin got on his horse and, parting regretfully from the peasants, rode homewards. On the hillside he looked back; he could not see them in the mist that had risen from the valley; he could only hear rough, good-humored voices, laughter, and the sound of clanking scythes.

Sergey Ivanovitch had long ago finished dinner, and was drinking iced lemon and water in his own room, looking through the reviews and papers which he had only just received by post, when Levin rushed into the room, talking merrily, with his wet and matted hair sticking to his forehead, and his back and chest grimed and moist.
"We mowed the whole meadow! Oh, it is nice, delicious! And how have you been getting on?" said Levin, completely forgetting the disagreeable conversation of the previous day.

"Mercy! what do you look like!" said Sergey Ivanovitch, for the first moment looking round with some dissatisfaction. "And the door, do shut the door!" he cried. "You must have let in a dozen at least."
Sergey Ivanovitch could not endure flies, and in his own room he never opened the window except at night, and carefully kept the door shut.
"Not one, on my honor. But if I have, I'll catch them. You wouldn't believe what a pleasure it is! How have you spent the day?"
"Very well. But have you really been mowing the whole day? I expect you're as hungry as a wolf. Kouzma has got everything ready for you."
"No, I don't feel hungry even. I had something to eat there. But I'll go and wash."

"Yes, go along, go along, and I'll come to you directly," said Sergey Ivanovitch, shaking his head as he looked at his brother. "Go along, make haste," he added smiling, and gathering up his books, he prepared to go too. He, too, felt suddenly good-humored and disinclined to leave his brother's side. "But what did you do while it was raining?"
"Rain? Why, there was scarcely a drop. I'll come directly. So you had a nice day too? That's first-rate." And Levin went off to change his clothes.

Five minutes later the brothers met in the dining-room. Although it seemed to Levin that he was not hungry, and he sat down to dinner simply so as not to hurt Kouzma's feelings, yet when he began to eat the dinner struck him as extraordinarily good. Sergey Ivanovitch watched him with a smile.
"Oh, by the way, there's a letter for you," said he. "Kouzma, bring it down, please. And mind you shut the doors."

The letter was from Oblonsky. Levin read it aloud. Oblonsky wrote to him from Petersburg: "I have had a letter from Dolly; she's at Ergushovo, and everything seems going wrong there. Do ride over and see her, please; help her with advice; you know all about it. She will be so glad to see you. She's quite alone, poor thing. My mother-in-law and all of them are still abroad."
"That's capital! I will certainly ride over to her," said Levin. "Or we'll go together. She's such a splendid woman, isn't she?"
"They're not far from here, then?"
"Twenty-five miles. Or perhaps it is thirty. But a capital road. Capital, we'll drive over."
"I shall be delighted," said Sergey Ivanovitch, still smiling. The sight of his younger brother's appearance had immediately put him in a good humor.
"Well, you have an appetite!" he said, looking at his dark-red, sunburnt face and neck bent over the plate.
"Splendid! You can't imagine what an effectual remedy it is for every sort of foolishness. I want to enrich medicine with a new word: _Arbeitskur_."
"Well, but you don't need it, I should fancy."
"No, but for all sorts of nervous invalids."

"Yes, it ought to be tried. I had meant to come to the mowing to look at you, but it was so unbearably hot that I got no further than the forest. I sat there a little, and went on by the forest to the village, met your old nurse, and sounded her as to the peasants' view of you. As far as I can make out, they don't approve of this. She said: 'It's not a gentleman's work.' Altogether, I fancy that in the people's ideas there are very clear and definite notions of certain, as they call it, 'gentlemanly' lines of action. And they don't sanction the gentry's moving outside bounds clearly laid down in their ideas."

"Maybe so; but anyway it's a pleasure such as I have never known in my life. And there's no harm in it, you know. Is there?" answered Levin. "I can't help it if they don't like it. Though I do believe it's all right. Eh?"
"Altogether," pursued Sergey Ivanovitch, "you're satisfied with your day?"
"Quite satisfied. We cut the whole meadow. And such a splendid old man I made friends with there! You can't fancy how delightful he was!"

"Well, so you're content with your day. And so am I. First, I solved two chess problems, and one a very pretty one—a pawn opening. I'll show it you. And then—I thought over our conversation yesterday."

"Eh! our conversation yesterday?" said Levin, blissfully dropping his eyelids and drawing deep breaths after finishing his dinner, and absolutely incapable of recalling what their conversation yesterday was about.

"I think you are partly right. Our difference of opinion amounts to this, that you make the mainspring self-interest, while I suppose that interest in the common weal is bound to exist in every man of a certain degree of advancement. Possibly you are right too, that action founded on material interest would be more desirable. You are altogether, as the French say, too _primesautière_ a nature; you must have intense, energetic action, or nothing."

Levin listened to his brother and did not understand a single word, and did not want to understand. He was only afraid his brother might ask him some question which would make it evident he had not heard.
"So that's what I think it is, my dear boy," said Sergey Ivanovitch, touching him on the shoulder.

"Yes, of course. But, do you know? I won't stand up for my view," answered Levin, with a guilty, childlike smile. "Whatever was it I was disputing about?" he wondered. "Of course, I'm right, and he's right, and it's all first-rate. Only I must go round to the counting house and see to things." He got up, stretching and smiling. Sergey Ivanovitch smiled too.

"If you want to go out, let's go together," he said, disinclined to be parted from his brother, who seemed positively breathing out freshness and energy. "Come, we'll go to the counting house, if you have to go there."
"Oh, heavens!" shouted Levin, so loudly that Sergey Ivanovitch was quite frightened.
"What, what is the matter?"
"How's Agafea Mihalovna's hand?" said Levin, slapping himself on the head. "I'd positively forgotten her even."
"It's much better."
"Well, anyway I'll run down to her. Before you've time to get your hat on, I'll be back."
And he ran downstairs, clattering with his heels like a spring-rattle.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone to Petersburg to perform the most natural and essential official duty—so familiar to everyone in the government service, though incomprehensible to outsiders—that duty, but for which one could hardly be in government service, of reminding the ministry of his existence—and having, for the due performance of this rite, taken all the available cash from home, was gaily and agreeably spending his days at the races and in the summer villas. Meanwhile Dolly and the children had moved into the country, to cut down expenses as much as possible. She had gone to Ergushovo, the estate that had been her dowry, and the one where in spring the forest had been sold. It was nearly forty miles from Levin's Pokrovskoe. The big, old house at Ergushovo had been pulled down long ago, and the old prince had had the lodge done up and built on to. Twenty years before, when Dolly was a child, the lodge had been roomy and comfortable, though, like all lodges, it stood sideways to the entrance avenue, and faced the south. But by now this lodge was old and dilapidated. When Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone down in the spring to sell the forest, Dolly had begged him to look over the house and order what repairs might be needed. Stepan Arkadyevitch, like all unfaithful husbands indeed, was very solicitous for his wife's comfort, and he had himself looked over the house, and given instructions about everything that he considered necessary. What he considered necessary was to cover all the furniture with cretonne, to put up curtains, to weed the garden, to make a little bridge on the pond, and to plant flowers. But he forgot many other essential matters, the want of which greatly distressed Darya Alexandrovna later on.

In spite of Stepan Arkadyevitch's efforts to be an attentive father and husband, he never could keep in his mind that he had a wife and children. He had bachelor tastes, and it was in accordance with them that he shaped his life. On his return to Moscow he informed his wife with pride that everything was ready, that the house would be a little paradise, and that he advised her most certainly to go. His wife's staying away in the country was very agreeable to Stepan Arkadyevitch from every point of view: it did the children good, it decreased expenses, and it left him more at liberty. Darya Alexandrovna regarded staying in the country for the summer as essential for the children, especially for the little girl, who had not succeeded in regaining her strength after the scarlatina, and also as a means of escaping the petty humiliations, the little bills owing to the wood-merchant, the fishmonger, the shoemaker, which made her miserable. Besides this, she was pleased to go away to the country because she was dreaming of getting her sister Kitty to stay with her there. Kitty was to be back from abroad in the middle of the summer, and bathing had been prescribed for her. Kitty wrote that no prospect was so alluring as to spend the summer with Dolly at Ergushovo, full of childish associations for both of them.

The first days of her existence in the country were very hard for Dolly. She used to stay in the country as a child, and the impression she had retained of it was that the country was a refuge from all the unpleasantness of the town, that life there, though not luxurious—Dolly could easily make up her mind to that—was cheap and comfortable; that there was plenty of everything, everything was cheap, everything could be got, and children were happy. But now coming to the country as the head of a family, she perceived that it was all utterly unlike what she had fancied.

The day after their arrival there was a heavy fall of rain, and in the night the water came through in the corridor and in the nursery, so that the beds had to be carried into the drawing-room. There was no kitchen maid to be found; of the nine cows, it appeared from the words of the cowherd-woman that some were about to calve, others had just calved, others were old, and others again hard-uddered; there was not butter nor milk enough even for the children. There were no eggs. They could get no fowls; old, purplish, stringy cocks were all they had for roasting and boiling. Impossible to get women to scrub the floors—all were potato-hoeing. Driving was out of the question, because one of the horses was restive, and bolted in the shafts. There was no place where they could bathe; the whole of the river-bank was trampled by the cattle and open to the road; even walks were impossible, for the cattle strayed into the garden through a gap in the hedge, and there was one terrible bull, who bellowed, and therefore might be expected to gore somebody. There were no proper cupboards for their clothes; what cupboards there were either would not close at all, or burst open whenever anyone passed by them. There were no pots and pans; there was no copper in the washhouse, nor even an ironing-board in the maids' room.

Finding instead of peace and rest all these, from her point of view, fearful calamities, Darya Alexandrovna was at first in despair. She exerted herself to the utmost, felt the hopelessness of the position, and was every instant suppressing the tears that started into her eyes. The bailiff, a retired quartermaster, whom Stepan Arkadyevitch had taken a fancy to and had appointed bailiff on account of his handsome and respectful appearance as a hall-porter, showed no sympathy for Darya Alexandrovna's woes. He said respectfully, "nothing can be done, the peasants are such a wretched lot," and did nothing to help her.

The position seemed hopeless. But in the Oblonskys' household, as in all families indeed, there was one inconspicuous but most valuable and useful person, Marya Philimonovna. She soothed her mistress, assured her that everything would _come round_ (it was her expression, and Matvey had borrowed it from her), and without fuss or hurry proceeded to set to work herself. She had immediately made friends with the bailiff's wife, and on the very first day she drank tea with her and the bailiff under the acacias, and reviewed all the circumstances of the position. Very soon Marya Philimonovna had established her club, so to say, under the acacias, and there it was, in this club, consisting of the bailiff's wife, the village elder, and the counting-house clerk, that the difficulties of existence were gradually smoothed away, and in a week's time everything actually had come round. The roof was mended, a kitchen maid was found—a crony of the village elder's—hens were bought, the cows began giving milk, the garden hedge was stopped up with stakes, the carpenter made a mangle, hooks were put in the cupboards, and they ceased to burst open spontaneously, and an ironing-board covered with army cloth was placed across from the arm of a chair to the chest of drawers, and there was a smell of flatirons in the maids' room.

"Just see, now, and you were quite in despair," said Marya Philimonovna, pointing to the ironing-board. They even rigged up a bathing-shed of straw hurdles. Lily began to bathe, and Darya Alexandrovna began to realize, if only in part, her expectations, if not of a peaceful, at least of a comfortable, life in the country. Peaceful with six children Darya Alexandrovna could not be. One would fall ill, another might easily become so, a third would be without something necessary, a fourth would show symptoms of a bad disposition, and so on. Rare indeed were the brief periods of peace. But these cares and anxieties were for Darya Alexandrovna the sole happiness possible. Had it not been for them, she would have been left alone to brood over her husband who did not love her. And besides, hard though it was for the mother to bear the dread of illness, the illnesses themselves, and the grief of seeing signs of evil propensities in her children—the children themselves were even now repaying her in small joys for her sufferings. Those joys were so small that they passed unnoticed, like gold in sand, and at bad moments she could see nothing but the pain, nothing but sand; but there were good moments too when she saw nothing but the joy, nothing but gold.

Now in the solitude of the country, she began to be more and more frequently aware of those joys. Often, looking at them, she would make every possible effort to persuade herself that she was mistaken, that she as a mother was partial to her children. All the same, she could not help saying to herself that she had charming children, all six of them in different ways, but a set of children such as is not often to be met with, and she was happy in them, and proud of them.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Towards the end of May, when everything had been more or less satisfactorily arranged, she received her husband's answer to her complaints of the disorganized state of things in the country. He wrote begging her forgiveness for not having thought of everything before, and promised to come down at the first chance. This chance did not present itself, and till the beginning of June Darya Alexandrovna stayed alone in the country.

On the Sunday in St. Peter's week Darya Alexandrovna drove to mass for all her children to take the sacrament. Darya Alexandrovna in her intimate, philosophical talks with her sister, her mother, and her friends very often astonished them by the freedom of her views in regard to religion. She had a strange religion of transmigration of souls all her own, in which she had firm faith, troubling herself little about the dogmas of the Church. But in her family she was strict in carrying out all that was required by the Church—and not merely in order to set an example, but with all her heart in it. The fact that the children had not been at the sacrament for nearly a year worried her extremely, and with the full approval and sympathy of Marya Philimonovna she decided that this should take place now in the summer.

For several days before, Darya Alexandrovna was busily deliberating on how to dress all the children. Frocks were made or altered and washed, seams and flounces were let out, buttons were sewn on, and ribbons got ready. One dress, Tanya's, which the English governess had undertaken, cost Darya Alexandrovna much loss of temper. The English governess in altering it had made the seams in the wrong place, had taken up the sleeves too much, and altogether spoilt the dress. It was so narrow on Tanya's shoulders that it was quite painful to look at her. But Marya Philimonovna had the happy thought of putting in gussets, and adding a little shoulder-cape. The dress was set right, but there was nearly a quarrel with the English governess. On the morning, however, all was happily arranged, and towards ten o'clock—the time at which they had asked the priest to wait for them for the mass—the children in their new dresses, with beaming faces, stood on the step before the carriage waiting for their mother.

To the carriage, instead of the restive Raven, they had harnessed, thanks to the representations of Marya Philimonovna, the bailiff's horse, Brownie, and Darya Alexandrovna, delayed by anxiety over her own attire, came out and got in, dressed in a white muslin gown.

Darya Alexandrovna had done her hair, and dressed with care and excitement. In the old days she had dressed for her own sake to look pretty and be admired. Later on, as she got older, dress became more and more distasteful to her. She saw that she was losing her good looks. But now she began to feel pleasure and interest in dress again. Now she did not dress for her own sake, not for the sake of her own beauty, but simply that as the mother of those exquisite creatures she might not spoil the general effect. And looking at herself for the last time in the looking-glass she was satisfied with herself. She looked nice. Not nice as she would have wished to look nice in old days at a ball, but nice for the object which she now had in view.

In the church there was no one but the peasants, the servants and their women-folk. But Darya Alexandrovna saw, or fancied she saw, the sensation produced by her children and her. The children were not only beautiful to look at in their smart little dresses, but they were charming in the way they behaved. Aliosha, it is true, did not stand quite correctly; he kept turning round, trying to look at his little jacket from behind; but all the same he was wonderfully sweet. Tanya behaved like a grown-up person, and looked after the little ones. And the smallest, Lily, was bewitching in her naïve astonishment at everything, and it was difficult not to smile when, after taking the sacrament, she said in English, "Please, some more."
On the way home the children felt that something solemn had happened, and were very sedate.

Everything went happily at home too; but at lunch Grisha began whistling, and, what was worse, was disobedient to the English governess, and was forbidden to have any tart. Darya Alexandrovna would not have let things go so far on such a day had she been present; but she had to support the English governess's authority, and she upheld her decision that Grisha should have no tart. This rather spoiled the general good humor. Grisha cried, declaring that Nikolinka had whistled too, and he was not punished, and that he wasn't crying for the tart—he didn't care—but at being unjustly treated. This was really too tragic, and Darya Alexandrovna made up her mind to persuade the English governess to forgive Grisha, and she went to speak to her. But on the way, as she passed the drawing-room, she beheld a scene, filling her heart with such pleasure that the tears came into her eyes, and she forgave the delinquent herself.

The culprit was sitting at the window in the corner of the drawing-room; beside him was standing Tanya with a plate. On the pretext of wanting to give some dinner to her dolls, she had asked the governess's permission to take her share of tart to the nursery, and had taken it instead to her brother. While still weeping over the injustice of his punishment, he was eating the tart, and kept saying through his sobs, "Eat yourself; let's eat it together ... together."
Tanya had at first been under the influence of her pity for Grisha, then of a sense of her noble action, and tears were standing in her eyes too; but she did not refuse, and ate her share.

On catching sight of their mother they were dismayed, but, looking into her face, they saw they were not doing wrong. They burst out laughing, and, with their mouths full of tart, they began wiping their smiling lips with their hands, and smearing their radiant faces all over with tears and jam.
"Mercy! Your new white frock! Tanya! Grisha!" said their mother, trying to save the frock, but with tears in her eyes, smiling a blissful, rapturous smile.

The new frocks were taken off, and orders were given for the little girls to have their blouses put on, and the boys their old jackets, and the wagonette to be harnessed; with Brownie, to the bailiff's annoyance, again in the shafts, to drive out for mushroom picking and bathing. A roar of delighted shrieks arose in the nursery, and never ceased till they had set off for the bathing-place.

They gathered a whole basketful of mushrooms; even Lily found a birch mushroom. It had always happened before that Miss Hoole found them and pointed them out to her; but this time she found a big one quite of herself, and there was a general scream of delight, "Lily has found a mushroom!"

Then they reached the river, put the horses under the birch trees, and went to the bathing-place. The coachman, Terenty, fastened the horses, who kept whisking away the flies, to a tree, and, treading down the grass, lay down in the shade of a birch and smoked his shag, while the never-ceasing shrieks of delight of the children floated across to him from the bathing-place.

Though it was hard work to look after all the children and restrain their wild pranks, though it was difficult too to keep in one's head and not mix up all the stockings, little breeches, and shoes for the different legs, and to undo and to do up again all the tapes and buttons, Darya Alexandrovna, who had always liked bathing herself, and believed it to be very good for the children, enjoyed nothing so much as bathing with all the children. To go over all those fat little legs, pulling on their stockings, to take in her arms and dip those little naked bodies, and to hear their screams of delight and alarm, to see the breathless faces with wide-open, scared, and happy eyes of all her splashing cherubs, was a great pleasure to her.

When half the children had been dressed, some peasant women in holiday dress, out picking herbs, came up to the bathing-shed and stopped shyly. Marya Philimonovna called one of them and handed her a sheet and a shirt that had dropped into the water for her to dry them, and Darya Alexandrovna began to talk to the women. At first they laughed behind their hands and did not understand her questions, but soon they grew bolder and began to talk, winning Darya Alexandrovna's heart at once by the genuine admiration of the children that they showed.
"My, what a beauty! as white as sugar," said one, admiring Tanitchka, and shaking her head; "but thin...."
"Yes, she has been ill."
"And so they've been bathing you too," said another to the baby.
"No; he's only three months old," answered Darya Alexandrovna with pride.
"You don't say so!"
"And have you any children?"
"I've had four; I've two living—a boy and a girl. I weaned her last carnival."
"How old is she?"
"Why, two years old."
"Why did you nurse her so long?"
"It's our custom; for three fasts...."
And the conversation became most interesting to Darya Alexandrovna. What sort of time did she have? What was the matter with the boy? Where was her husband? Did it often happen?

Darya Alexandrovna felt disinclined to leave the peasant women, so interesting to her was their conversation, so completely identical were all their interests. What pleased her most of all was that she saw clearly what all the women admired more than anything was her having so many children, and such fine ones. The peasant women even made Darya Alexandrovna laugh, and offended the English governess, because she was the cause of the laughter she did not understand. One of the younger women kept staring at the Englishwoman, who was dressing after all the rest, and when she put on her third petticoat she could not refrain from the remark, "My, she keeps putting on and putting on, and she'll never have done!" she said, and they all went off into roars.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: On the drive home, as Darya Alexandrovna, with all her children round her, their heads still wet from their bath, and a kerchief tied over her own head, was getting near the house, the coachman said, "There's some gentleman coming: the master of Pokrovskoe, I do believe."

Darya Alexandrovna peeped out in front, and was delighted when she recognized in the gray hat and gray coat the familiar figure of Levin walking to meet them. She was glad to see him at any time, but at this moment she was specially glad he should see her in all her glory. No one was better able to appreciate her grandeur than Levin.
Seeing her, he found himself face to face with one of the pictures of his daydream of family life.
"You're like a hen with your chickens, Darya Alexandrovna."
"Ah, how glad I am to see you!" she said, holding out her hand to him.
"Glad to see me, but you didn't let me know. My brother's staying with me. I got a note from Stiva that you were here."
"From Stiva?" Darya Alexandrovna asked with surprise.

"Yes; he writes that you are here, and that he thinks you might allow me to be of use to you," said Levin, and as he said it he became suddenly embarrassed, and, stopping abruptly, he walked on in silence by the wagonette, snapping off the buds of the lime trees and nibbling them. He was embarrassed through a sense that Darya Alexandrovna would be annoyed by receiving from an outsider help that should by rights have come from her own husband. Darya Alexandrovna certainly did not like this little way of Stepan Arkadyevitch's of foisting his domestic duties on others. And she was at once aware that Levin was aware of this. It was just for this fineness of perception, for this delicacy, that Darya Alexandrovna liked Levin.

"I know, of course," said Levin, "that that simply means that you would like to see me, and I'm exceedingly glad. Though I can fancy that, used to town housekeeping as you are, you must feel in the wilds here, and if there's anything wanted, I'm altogether at your disposal."

"Oh, no!" said Dolly. "At first things were rather uncomfortable, but now we've settled everything capitally—thanks to my old nurse," she said, indicating Marya Philimonovna, who, seeing that they were speaking of her, smiled brightly and cordially to Levin. She knew him, and knew that he would be a good match for her young lady, and was very keen to see the matter settled.
"Won't you get in, sir, we'll make room this side!" she said to him.

"No, I'll walk. Children, who'd like to race the horses with me?" The children knew Levin very little, and could not remember when they had seen him, but they experienced in regard to him none of that strange feeling of shyness and hostility which children so often experience towards hypocritical, grown-up people, and for which they are so often and miserably punished. Hypocrisy in anything whatever may deceive the cleverest and most penetrating man, but the least wide-awake of children recognizes it, and is revolted by it, however ingeniously it may be disguised. Whatever faults Levin had, there was not a trace of hypocrisy in him, and so the children showed him the same friendliness that they saw in their mother's face. On his invitation, the two elder ones at once jumped out to him and ran with him as simply as they would have done with their nurse or Miss Hoole or their mother. Lily, too, began begging to go to him, and her mother handed her to him; he sat her on his shoulder and ran along with her.
"Don't be afraid, don't be afraid, Darya Alexandrovna!" he said, smiling good-humoredly to the mother; "there's no chance of my hurting or dropping her."
And, looking at his strong, agile, assiduously careful and needlessly wary movements, the mother felt her mind at rest, and smiled gaily and approvingly as she watched him.

Here, in the country, with children, and with Darya Alexandrovna, with whom he was in sympathy, Levin was in a mood not infrequent with him, of childlike light-heartedness that she particularly liked in him. As he ran with the children, he taught them gymnastic feats, set Miss Hoole laughing with his queer English accent, and talked to Darya Alexandrovna of his pursuits in the country.
After dinner, Darya Alexandrovna, sitting alone with him on the balcony, began to speak of Kitty.
"You know, Kitty's coming here, and is going to spend the summer with me."

"Really," he said, flushing, and at once, to change the conversation, he said: "Then I'll send you two cows, shall I? If you insist on a bill you shall pay me five roubles a month; but it's really too bad of you."
"No, thank you. We can manage very well now."
"Oh, well, then, I'll have a look at your cows, and if you'll allow me, I'll give directions about their food. Everything depends on their food."

And Levin, to turn the conversation, explained to Darya Alexandrovna the theory of cow-keeping, based on the principle that the cow is simply a machine for the transformation of food into milk, and so on.
He talked of this, and passionately longed to hear more of Kitty, and, at the same time, was afraid of hearing it. He dreaded the breaking up of the inward peace he had gained with such effort.
"Yes, but still all this has to be looked after, and who is there to look after it?" Darya Alexandrovna responded, without interest.

She had by now got her household matters so satisfactorily arranged, thanks to Marya Philimonovna, that she was disinclined to make any change in them; besides, she had no faith in Levin's knowledge of farming. General principles, as to the cow being a machine for the production of milk, she looked on with suspicion. It seemed to her that such principles could only be a hindrance in farm management. It all seemed to her a far simpler matter: all that was needed, as Marya Philimonovna had explained, was to give Brindle and Whitebreast more food and drink, and not to let the cook carry all the kitchen slops to the laundry maid's cow. That was clear. But general propositions as to feeding on meal and on grass were doubtful and obscure. And, what was most important, she wanted to talk about Kitty.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: "Kitty writes to me that there's nothing she longs for so much as quiet and solitude," Dolly said after the silence that had followed.
"And how is she—better?" Levin asked in agitation.
